title: Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models

paper.title: Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models
paper.abstract:
Abstract Despite the success of discrete diffusion language models (dLMs) for fast parallel decoding, their non-smooth, high-dimensional space hinders trajectory steering for reasoning and inference acceleration. To overcome this, we present Sigma , the first large-scale (3B/8B) continuous dLM built on steerable, low-dimensional ODE/SDE latent trajectories. Trained blockwise via likelihood optimization, Sigma jointly denoises Gaussian-corrupted token embeddings while learning an optimal embedding geometry. To accelerate training, Sigma leverages pre-trained weights from autoregressive (AR) models for warm-starting. During inference, we identify classifier-free guidance and score temperature as essential for high-fidelity reasoning and coding. Across comprehensive math reasoning and coding evaluations against state-of-the-art discrete counterparts (masked dLMs and AR baselines), Sigma achieves competitive performance with discrete models on standard benchmarks (e.g., GSM8K, Minerva, HumanEval, MBPP) after pre-training and on challenging reasoning tasks (e.g., MATH-500, AIME) after supervised fine-tuning. Beyond performance parity, we uncover key structural properties unique to continuous dLMs: ( i ) embedding-space steering effectively governs the quality-diversity trade-off, yielding strong pass@ k k performance
and
( ii ) continuous trajectories enable graceful degradation for low NFEs and efficient distillation. These establish continuous dLMs as a promising paradigm for efficient language generation.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: While diffusion language models (dLMs) enable fast parallel decoding compared to autoregressive (AR) baselines ( Inception Labs et al., 2025 ; Song et al., 2025 ; Fu et al., 2026 ) , dominant discrete dLMs operate in high-dimensional, categorical state spaces (e.g., V ≥ 100 ​ K V{\geq}100\text{K} ) that suffer under limited step budgets and impede trajectory control for complex reasoning and coding tasks. Continuous diffusion offers a principled way to overcome these structural limitations through smooth latent geometries that natively support structured editing ( Meng et al., 2022 ) , flexible ODE trajectory steering ( Lu et al., 2022 ) , and efficient few-step distillation ( Salimans and Ho, 2022 ; Song et al., 2023 ) . Recently, there has been growing interest in continuous diffusion and flow matching for text generation ( Gulrajani and Hashimoto, 2023 ; Dieleman et al., 2022 ; Hu et al., 2026 ; Lee et al., 2026 ; Guo et al., 2026 ; Liang et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026 ) ; see App. A . However, existing methods remain limited in scale ( < 2 ​ B <2\text{B} ) or focus on unconditional generation, lacking evaluations on complex reasoning tasks. Whether continuous dLMs scale to complex conditional reasoning remains open. This is a non-trivial hurdle because continuous models update block embeddings globally, in contrast to the factorized categorical denoising of discrete dLMs that leads to semi-autoregressive token commitment per block. To overcome these limitations, we present Sigma (3B/8B): s cal i ng up G aussian diffusion m odels for l a nguage. We propose a family of continuous dLMs operating over a 16-dimensional embedding space trained blockwise via likelihood optimization. Within each block, the model learns to jointly denoise Gaussian-corrupted token embeddings and to structure an optimal embedding geometry. To scale training, we warm-start the model from existing pre-trained AR weights. For inference, we explore diffusion trajectory sampling, identifying embedding-space Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) and Score Temperature (ST) as crucial ingredients for high-fidelity reasoning and coding. Figure 1 : Left: Inference pipeline. Sigma generates text blockwise via iterative diffusion denoising over 16D continuous latents ( 𝐳 t \mathbf{z}_{t} ) conditioned on a KV-cached prefix ( 𝐜 \mathbf{c} ), followed by categorical readout. Predicted vocabulary probabilities 𝐱 θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , 𝐜 ) \mathbf{x}_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t;\mathbf{c}) map to mean predictions 𝐞 θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , 𝐜 ) \mathbf{e}_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t;\mathbf{c}) in 16D space via categorical reparameterization. Clean embeddings (dots) lie on the 16D unit sphere, while 𝐞 θ \mathbf{e}_{\theta} lies on or within it. Middle: Smooth trajectory enables low-NFE reasoning. GSM8K accuracy vs. NFEs using the optimal sampler per step budget (PDD: Parallel Decoding Distillation). Right: Scaling inference-time compute. Pass@ k k vs. k k on AIME 2025 (solid curves: fixed config across k k ; thin curves: alternative tested configs). Through unified evaluations against state-of-the-art discrete dLMs (e.g., Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion ( Fu et al., 2026 ) , LLaDA ( Nie et al., 2025b ) , Dream ( Ye et al., 2025 ) , SDAR ( Cheng et al., 2026 ) ), we show that Sigma achieves competitive performance across standard math and coding benchmarks (e.g., GSM8K, Minerva, HumanEval, MBPP) and extends well to harder reasoning tasks after supervised fine-tuning (e.g., MATH-500, AIME). Beyond raw accuracy, we highlight two structural properties unique to continuous language diffusion: ( i ) flexible pass@ k k exploration–exploitation control via CFG and ST hyperparameters; and ( ii ) graceful performance degradation under low NFE regimes (16/32) and efficient trajectory distillation for very low NFE regimes (4/8). Together, these properties position continuous diffusion as a promising foundation for fast inference in modern agentic AI. Our key contributions are summarized as follows: • First Large-Scale Continuous dLM: We present Sigma (3B/8B), efficiently trained by warm-starting from pre-trained AR weights, and optimizing a regularized continuous diffusion ELBO. • Competitive Math & Coding: Across six base and ten instruct benchmarks, Sigma achieves competitive performance with state-of-the-art discrete dLMs/ARs on reasoning and coding. • Inference Steering (CFG & ST): By elucidating the inference design space, we show that embedding-space CFG and ST effectively govern the quality-diversity trade-off with minimal latency overhead via single-pass block-causal attention packing. • Low-NFE Robustness: With embedding regularization, Sigma sustains strong quality down to 16 NFEs per block, while trajectory distillation noticeably improves performance at 4–8 NFEs.

sections.heading: Learned embeddings.
sections.text: The NELBO 2 depends on 𝐄 {\mathbf{E}} via 1 , where embeddings become likelihood-trained parameters, which separates Plaid from continuous dLMs built on fixed (e.g., one-hot) encodings. Not learning embeddings significantly worsens Plaid’s performance ( Yang et al., 2026 ) .

sections.heading: Self-conditioning (SC).
sections.text: Proposed in Chen et al. (2023) , SC lets the denoiser see its own previous estimate. Let 𝐱 θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , 𝐞 sc ) {\mathbf{x}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{z}}_{t},t;{\mathbf{e}}_{\text{sc}}) denote a denoiser taking an additional predicted clean embedding 𝐞 sc ∈ ℝ L × d e {\mathbf{e}}_{\text{sc}}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d_{e}} , and 𝟎 {\mathbf{0}} for the empty condition (omitted by default in our notation). During training, 25 % 25\% of training samples are self-conditioned: a first pass without gradient tracking produces 𝐞 sc := 𝐱 θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , 𝟎 ) ​ 𝐄 {\mathbf{e}}_{\text{sc}}:={\mathbf{x}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{z}}_{t},t;{\mathbf{0}}){\mathbf{E}} , and only the second pass, 𝐱 θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , sg ⁡ ( 𝐞 sc ) ) ​ 𝐄 {\mathbf{x}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{z}}_{t},t;\operatorname{sg}({\mathbf{e}}_{\text{sc}})){\mathbf{E}} , receives gradients. The remaining samples use 𝟎 {\mathbf{0}} as SC input, so the denoiser learns both branches. During validation, all samples enable SC. Since 𝐞 sc {\mathbf{e}}_{\text{sc}} is itself a function of ( 𝐳 t , t ) ({\mathbf{z}}_{t},t) , the NELBO remains valid. Notice that during training, 25 % 25\% SC increases the non-embedding FLOPs by only about 8 % 8\% , which is minimal. Furthermore, during inference, one directly feeds the previous-step’s prediction as SC, which incurs no overhead.

sections.heading: Scaling.
sections.text: RePlaid ( Yang et al., 2026 ) realigns Plaid with the architectures of modern discrete dLMs/ARs and finds that, once aligned, continuous diffusion scales competitively with masked diffusion.

sections.text: (a) Training procedure of Sigma . (b) Attention mask for training. Figure 2 : Training procedure of Sigma (a) and its transformer attention mask (b) for an example sequence 𝐱 {\mathbf{x}} of length L = 6 L=6 with block size L ′ = 2 L^{\prime}=2 . During pre-training, we feed the clean discrete tokens 𝐱 \mathbf{x} to the AR stream (a, left part) and the noisy continuous embeddings 𝐳 \mathbf{z} to the diffusion stream (a, right part). For the diffusion stream, each block is randomly chosen to either compute the reconstruction loss (1st block, t = 0 t=0 ) or the diffusion loss (2nd & 3rd blocks, t ∼ Unif ⁡ [ 0 , 1 ] t\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,1] ); see 5 . Reconstruction loss is the cross entropy between the logits and the ground truth tokens, while for diffusion loss we use categorical reparameterization to obtain the mean embedding prediction and compute the mean squared error against the ground truth diffusion embeddings.

sections.heading: 3.2 Pre-Training
sections.text: NLD utilizes AR initialization and regularization to enhance downstream performance ( Fu et al., 2026 ) . However, adapting these techniques to continuous dLMs like Sigma is non-trivial, as the activation dynamics of continuous and discrete models differ fundamentally; it is thus unclear whether discrete AR initialization remains as effective for continuous representation space. To establish a rigorous baseline, we first align Sigma ’s data, architecture, and optimization with discrete dLMs for a controlled comparison at scale ( Sec. 3.2.1 ). In Sec. 3.2.2 , we evaluate the impact of AR initialization when pre-training Sigma -3B with 3 , followed by an investigation of AR regularization for training our flagship 3B/8B models. (a) From scratch + no AR reg. Block size: 64 (b) From AR init. + no AR reg. Block size: 64 (c) From AR init. + AR reg. Block size: 32 Figure 3 : Pre-training Sigma -3B from scratch (a), from AR initialization (b), and from AR initialization with AR regularization (c). PPL for AR and diffusion streams is computed via ℒ ar ​ ( 𝐱 ) \mathcal{L}_{\text{ar}}({\mathbf{x}}) 6 and ℒ BD ​ ( 𝐱 ) \mathcal{L}_{\text{BD}}({\mathbf{x}}) 3 , respectively. Early investigations (a, b) used block size 64; our flagship 3B model (c) used block size 32 to match the inference block size of NLD. Proper AR initialization/regularization leads to the best Sigma model.

sections.heading: Data.
sections.text: As with NLD, we adopt the open-sourced pre-training data from Basant et al. (2025) . We use the Mistral-NeMo tokenizer ( V = 131,072 V=131{,}072 ) ( Mistral AI, 2024 ) , batch size 512 512 , and L = 4096 L=4096 .

sections.heading: Architecture.
sections.text: Sigma adopts the transformer backbone of NLD and its AR baseline, ensuring the three families are parameter- and FLOP-matched. As with NLD, Sigma uses a block causal attention mask ( Fig. 2(b) ). Sigma uniquely adds a unit-norm 16-dimensional diffusion embedding table with a linear up-projection, a categorical reparameterization mapping V V -dimensional probabilities to low-dimensional soft embeddings, a self-conditioning linear projection, Fourier time conditioning, and a learnable noise schedule (see Sec. 2 ). Together, these account for less than 1 % 1\% of the total parameters. We provide thorough details in App. E .

sections.heading: Training.
sections.text: We train our models for 150K steps, following the optimization procedure detailed in App. E . Given a batch size of 512, 150K steps correspond to over 300B tokens. Training consumed ~9,600 and ~19,200 NVIDIA GB200 GPU hours for the 3B and 8B models, respectively.

sections.heading: AR Initialization.
sections.text: To evaluate the impact of initialization, we compare pre-training Sigma ( i ) from scratch and ( ii ) from an AR baseline pretrained on 1T tokens. Due to the dimension mismatch between high-dimensional AR embeddings and Sigma ’s 16-dimensional space, we randomly initialize the diffusion embedding layer. As shown in Figs. 3(a) and 3(b) , Sigma -3B ( L ′ = 64 L^{\prime}{=}64 ) with self-conditioning achieves competitive perplexity relative to NLD-3B ( L ′ = 64 L^{\prime}{=}64 ) under both regimes (i) and (ii). However, AR initialization significantly accelerates convergence and yields lower final training loss.

sections.heading: AR Regularization.
sections.text: Continuous diffusion training inherently suffers from high gradient variance and slow convergence. To mitigate variance and accelerate optimization, we follow NLD by adding AR regularization, optimizing the joint objective ℒ ar + w diff ​ ℒ BD \mathcal{L}_{\text{ar}}+w_{\text{diff}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{BD}} ( Fig. 3(c) ; see App. E for the w diff w_{\text{diff}} weighting schedule), where ℒ ar = ∑ l = 2 L − log ⟨ 𝐱 θ l ( 𝐱 < l ) , 𝐱 l ⟩ \mathcal{L}_{\text{ar}}={\textstyle\sum}_{l=2}^{L}-\log\langle{\mathbf{x}}_{\theta}^{l}({\mathbf{x}}^{<l}),{\mathbf{x}}^{l}\rangle (6) is computed over the AR stream using causal attention ( Fig. 2 ). This architecture employs two distinct readout heads, with the AR regularization computed exclusively from the AR head. While this dual-head formulation improves auxiliary AR decoding capability, our primary objective remains maximizing diffusion decoding performance. Finally, input sequences utilize AR embeddings for the AR stream and 16D diffusion embeddings for the diffusion stream ( Fig. 2 ), facilitating AR initialization and efficient KV-caching. As shown in Fig. 3(c) , AR regularization significantly improves training stability; with a properly tuned w diff w_{\text{diff}} , it even outperforms pure perplexity optimization for the diffusion stream. This confirms that AR regularization stabilizes training while yielding a higher-quality model. Consequently, we adopt AR initialization, AR regularization, and a block size of L ′ = 32 L^{\prime}{=}32 for all subsequent Sigma experiments.

sections.heading: 4 Language Generation via Continuous Diffusion Sampling
sections.text: Drawing on the success of continuous diffusion samplers using SDE/ODE solvers ( Song et al., 2021b ) , we systematically explore decoding samplers for continuous dLMs, evaluating performance across standard mathematical reasoning and coding benchmarks.

sections.heading: 4.1 Block diffusion sampling
sections.text: To generate a response 𝐫 {\mathbf{r}} given a prompt 𝐩 {\mathbf{p}} , we denoise one block at a time. Let 𝐜 := ( 𝐩 , 𝐫 ( < b ) ) {\mathbf{c}}:=({\mathbf{p}},{\mathbf{r}}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}<b})}) be the clean context available when generating block b b , stored in an attention key-value (KV) cache using the AR embeddings. An offset block-causal mask determines who can see whom ( Fig. 4(a) ). Positions in 𝐜 {\mathbf{c}} use causal attention, so their KV can be cached and reused across diffusion steps, regardless of whether the prompt length is a multiple of L ′ L^{\prime} . Positions in the noisy block 𝐳 t ( b ) {\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})} attend bidirectionally within the block and causally to the entire prefix 𝐜 {\mathbf{c}} . After a block is decoded, the AR embeddings of its committed tokens are appended to the causal KV cache for the next block during the next block’s first diffusion step, without incurring an extra NFE. See Alg. 2 for the complete sampling algorithm. Note that, in subsequent analysis, we do not account for this extra decoding step as a part of the diffusion sampling budget.

sections.heading: 4.2 Trajectory Steering
sections.text: To sharpen model predictions, we incorporate two reverse-process steering methods to our blockwise continuous diffusion model with no impact to its training efficiency and minimal impact to its inference efficiency.

sections.heading: Classifier-free guidance (CFG).
sections.text: CFG ( Ho and Salimans, 2022 ) is the standard tool for class-conditional or text-to-image diffusion models. In CFG, one queries the model twice to obtain a conditional and an unconditional prediction and then linearly extrapolates them. For our block diffusion model, the clean context 𝐜 {\mathbf{c}} serves as the natural conditioning information, and CFG extrapolates away from the unconditional prediction for the current block b {\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b} : 𝐞 θ w ​ ( 𝐳 t ( b ) , t , 𝐜 ) := 𝐞 θ ​ ( 𝐳 t ( b ) , t , ∅ ) + w ⁡ [ 𝐞 θ ​ ( 𝐳 t ( b ) , t , 𝐜 ) − 𝐞 θ ​ ( 𝐳 t ( b ) , t , ∅ ) ] , \displaystyle{\mathbf{e}}^{w}_{\theta}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})},t;{\mathbf{c}}):={\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})},t;\varnothing)+w\,\big[{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})},t;{\mathbf{c}})-{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})},t;\varnothing)\big], (CFG) where ∅ \varnothing drops the entire clean context 𝐜 {\mathbf{c}} (so 𝐳 t ( b ) {\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})} attends only within its own block) and w ≥ 1 w\geq 1 is the guidance strength ( w = 1 w=1 falls back to the plain conditional prediction). We bring two technical considerations. First, at batch size 1 1 transformer inference is memory-bound, so we pack conditional and unconditional predictions into a single forward pass at almost no wall-clock cost ( Liu et al., 2026b ) , using the packed mask of Fig. 4(a) . We measure this overhead to be less than 5 % 5\% per forward pass at block size 32 32 and 64 64 ( Sec. G.10 ). Second, unlike in image diffusion models and existing dLMs that require train-time context dropout ( Potaptchik et al., 2026 ; Hu et al., 2026 ) , our CFG is a pure inference-time trick : due to sequence packing in pre-training, the first block typically starts in the middle of a document and naturally sees no context. We discuss existing approaches in App. A .

sections.text: ST ( Dieleman et al., 2022 ) is a heuristic that sharpens the conditional score itself, rescaling the score ∇ log ⁡ p t ​ ( 𝐳 t ( b ) | 𝐜 ) \nabla\log p_{t}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})}|{\mathbf{c}}) (or equivalently, the noise prediction) by 1 τ \frac{1}{\tau} for τ ∈ ( 0 , 1 ] \tau\in(0,1] . One can show that it corresponds to the following operation on the mean prediction. 𝐞 θ τ ​ ( 𝐳 t ( b ) , t , 𝐜 ) := 𝐳 t ( b ) α t + 1 τ ​ [ 𝐞 θ ​ ( 𝐳 t ( b ) , t , 𝐜 ) − 𝐳 t ( b ) α t ] . \displaystyle{\mathbf{e}}^{\tau}_{\theta}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})},t;{\mathbf{c}}):=\tfrac{{\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})}}{\alpha_{t}}+\tfrac{1}{\tau}\big[{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})},t;{\mathbf{c}})-\tfrac{{\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})}}{\alpha_{t}}\big]. (ST) Intuitively, since 𝔼 ⁡ [ 𝐳 t ( b ) | 𝐱 ( b ) ] = α t ​ 𝐞 ( b ) \E[{\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})}|{\mathbf{x}}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})}]=\alpha_{t}{\mathbf{e}}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})} , 1 α t ​ 𝐳 t ( b ) \frac{1}{\alpha_{t}}{\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})} serves as the naive bad prediction to extrapolate from. ST does not incur further model queries, and τ = 1 \tau=1 leaves the sampler unchanged. We also recognize ST as a special case of Temporal Score Rescaling proposed in ( Xu et al., 2026 ) . CFG and ST mix the two denoisers into 𝐞 θ w , τ {\mathbf{e}}^{w,\tau}_{\theta} ; an update yields 𝐳 s ( b ) {\mathbf{z}}_{s}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})} . Combining both techniques yields larger gains over applying either in isolation, and markedly outperforms sampling without CFG or ST. See Fig. 10 for the full tuning grid. Finally, we remark that due to the commutativity of CFG and ST , we can combine them into a single operation 𝐞 θ w , τ ​ ( 𝐳 t ( b ) , t , 𝐜 ) {\mathbf{e}}^{w,\tau}_{\theta}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})},t;{\mathbf{c}}) , which is essentially using the score of the composed distribution ( p t ( ⋅ ∣ 𝐜 ) w p t ( ⋅ ∣ ∅ ) 1 − w ) 1 / τ (p_{t}(\cdot\mid{\mathbf{c}})^{w}p_{t}(\cdot\mid\varnothing)^{1-w})^{1/\tau} ( Prop. 1 ). We observed that using either knob is weaker than using both of them, see Fig. 5 .

sections.heading: Self-conditioning (SC).
sections.text: At inference, SC is applied only to the conditional prediction: when querying the model at time s s , the previous step’s conditional prediction 𝐞 θ ​ ( 𝐳 t ( b ) , t , 𝐜 ) {\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})},t;{\mathbf{c}}) (before applying CFG and ST) serves as the SC input for the conditional prediction, while the unconditional prediction receives 𝟎 {\mathbf{0}} SC input ( Fig. 4(b) ).

sections.heading: Sharpening in logit space.
sections.text: While both knobs above act on the mean embedding prediction obtained after the categorical reparameterization, we can also sharpen in logit space by applying the same two ideas before the softmax. In Sec. G.3 , we show that the logit-space CFG and temperature do provide sharpening, but the embedding-space knobs provide stronger performance, hence we keep CFG and ST as the default option.

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: In AR mode, Sigma -3B attains the best six-task average across all methods; in diffusion mode, our DDPM-256 run is comparable to Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion-3B on average and sets the best base-model numbers on GSM8K, HumanEval, and HumanEval+ ; it also outperforms LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B by 22.6 22.6 and 5.6 5.6 points on average respectively, despite being ~ 2 × 2\times smaller in parameters. Empirically, we observe less left-to-right bias within a block for Sigma compared with the confidence-based masked dLM sampling ( Fig. 20 ). To confirm the benefit of AR regularization ( Sec. 3.2.2 ), we also trained Sigma -3B with just ℒ BD \mathcal{L}_{\text{BD}} 3 without ℒ ar \mathcal{L}_{\text{ar}} 6 ; results are uniformly worse across all tasks ( Fig. 11 ). sections.heading: Pass@ k k analysis.
sections.text: While pass@1 accuracy in Tab. 1 captures single-draw quality, test-time search and RL draw multiple rollouts for the same prompt, where diverse rollouts are needed for richer learning signals and increase the chance of discovering a correct solution. Pass@ k k does not directly measure diversity, but tests whether additional samples expand correct-solution coverage. We sweep CFG and ST for Sigma -3B and confidence threshold and sampling temperature for NLD, reporting each model’s best tested config at each budget k k . On MBPP, Sigma overtakes NLD at k = 32 k=32 and reaches 91.8 % 91.8\% versus 87.6 % 87.6\% at k = 256 k=256 ( Fig. 6 ). See Sec. G.8 for the full study.

sections.heading: 5.1 ODE Sampler and Time Discretization
sections.text: In previous results, we run 256 DDPM steps per block to establish the strongest performance. In low-NFE regime, it is generally known that deterministic samplers paired with well-tuned time discretization lead to better performance. To investigate the tradeoffs for Sigma -3B, we choose two representative tasks (GSM8K and HumanEval), and vary the sampler (DDPM or DDIM) and the time-discretization across various diffusion sampling budgets T ∈ { 4 , 8 , 16 , 32 , 64 , 128 , 256 } T\in\{4,8,16,32,64,128,256\} . For each sampler-discretization-budget combination, we sweep CFG and ST; we then report, for each combination, the CFG-ST pair that achieves the best average accuracy over the two tasks.

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: As shown in Fig. 13 , DDIM substantially outperforms DDPM at low NFEs while matching DDPM at high NFEs. The uniform- γ \gamma discretization ( Sec. G.6 ) performs the best for a wide range of budgets. The best CFG-ST pairs are shown in Fig. 14 . Surprisingly, we found that higher-order ODE solvers originally proposed for image diffusion models (e.g., Zhang and Chen (2023) ; Lu et al. (2022) ) perform worse than DDIM, see Sec. G.7 for the full study. Using the same optimal hyperparameters from the two tasks, we evaluate the 16/32-step performance across all six tasks in Tabs. 1 and 2 ; Tab. 8 shows performance at other budgets.

sections.heading: 5.2 Embedding Regularization
sections.text: We observe that during training, embeddings collapse to ~4 effective dimensions in terms of principal components—a phenomenon not typically seen in standard autoregressive language model embeddings. While the current model achieves strong high-NFE performance, we hypothesize that regularizing the embeddings to be more uniformly distributed on the unit sphere will improve low-NFE performance. Our intuition is that representation collapse exacerbates token ambiguity, particularly when coarse numerical precision and low-NFE sampling introduce prediction errors. To mitigate this, we apply Sketched Uniform Spherical Regularization (SUSReg, Nicollier et al. (2026) ) to the embedding matrix 𝐄 {\mathbf{E}} during pre-training, penalizing the deviation between its empirical distribution and a uniform distribution on the unit sphere (see Sec. E.1 ).

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: As shown in Figs. 7 and 8 , the resulting Sigma -SUSReg-3B improves few-step and distillation results compared to Sigma -3B. Interestingly, SUSReg brings nearly no penalty to the validation PPL, although the learned embedding geometry differs substantially from that learned without SUSReg ( Fig. 8 ).

sections.heading: 5.3 Parallel Decoding Distillation for Few-step Generation
sections.text: Although DDIM has better performance than DDPM at reduced denoising steps, the pretrained model still loses quality at very low NFEs with a clear drop-off below 16 NFEs ( Fig. 7 ). We therefore distill the many-step trajectory of Sigma -3B into a few-step student. Our method adapts Parallel Decoding Distillation (PDD, Shaul et al. (2026) ) to blockwise continuous language diffusion, see App. I for full details. Due to the parallel nature of the student PDD heads, they cannot utilize recurrent computation, so we distill from the teacher without self-conditioning (-SC). During distillation, we amortize CFG into our student by training the single conditional student call to match the two-call guided teacher directly, which reduces FLOPs during sampling.

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: As shown in Figs. 7 and 8 , PDD is most helpful at 4 diffusion NFEs and pre-training with SUSReg improves PDD performance .

sections.heading: 7 Conclusions
sections.text: We introduced Sigma , a blockwise continuous dLM via efficient continual pre-training from an AR checkpoint, together with a reverse-diffusion sampling recipe that combines DDPM/DDIM samplers with CFG, ST, and SC. Sigma (3B/8B), in diffusion mode, performs comparably with the same-size masked dLM (Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion) trained under an aligned pipeline. The same conclusions generally transfers to post-SFT. Moreover, we adapt a sphere-normalized embedding regularization technique and few-step distillation to Sigma , which together enable non-trivial 4/8-step results. We discuss limitations and future directions in App. B .

sections.heading: Appendix A Related Work
sections.text: [Back to Sec. 1 or Sec. 2 in the main paper.] This appendix provides a literature review on continuous diffusion language models, the family to which Sigma belongs.

sections.heading: Continuous diffusion language models.
sections.text: Continuous dLMs lift discrete tokens into a Euclidean space and run a Gaussian (or Riemannian) diffusion there. A central attraction for doing so is that the machinery developed for image diffusion, such as efficient ODE solvers, guidance, and distillation techniques, transfers with little modification. Existing methods differ mainly in where the diffusion process lives: • Diffusing token embeddings . Diffusion-LM ( Li et al., 2022 ) pioneered this approach with Gaussian diffusion over learned word embeddings and a rounding step back to tokens; CDCD ( Dieleman et al., 2022 ) refined the objective with score interpolation and a categorical cross-entropy loss over softmax logits, and self-conditioned embedding diffusion ( Strudel et al., 2022 ) added self-conditioning on the previous denoising estimate. Plaid ( Gulrajani and Hashimoto, 2023 ) tied these ideas together around a likelihood target by pairing low-dimensional sphere-normalized embeddings with a learned noise schedule and categorical reparameterization; RePlaid ( Yang et al., 2026 ) aligns this recipe with modern DiT architectures and shows it scales competitively with discrete dLMs. Meanwhile, LangFlow ( Chen et al., 2026b ) follows the same learnable-embedding but uses cross-entropy training loss, while Wu et al. (2026) adopts a stochastic-localization formulation. 𝕊 \mathbb{S} -FLM ( Deschenaux and Gulcehre, 2026 ) and Spherical Flows ( Chemseddine et al., 2026 ) likewise use learnable token embeddings but further constrain the diffusion trajectory itself to the embedding hypersphere. A parallel strand fixes the embedding to be one-hot rather than learned: FLM ( Lee et al., 2026 ) and DFM ( Potaptchik et al., 2026 ) run flow matching from a Gaussian source to one-hot vocabulary targets in ℝ V \mathbb{R}^{V} , and further distill the flow into a few-step flow map for fast generation. • Diffusing an autoencoded latent . Here, a text autoencoder produces a compact continuous latent variable and diffusion is run in that latent space. LD4LG ( Lovelace et al., 2023 ) runs latent diffusion on a frozen encoder–decoder (BART and T5); COSMOS ( Meshchaninov et al., 2025 ) , ELF ( Hu et al., 2026 ) Cola-DLM ( Guo et al., 2026 ) , and AURORA-LM ( Liang et al., 2026 ) scale this axis with different latent designs and training objectives; LDLM ( Meshchaninov et al., 2026 ) learns the encoder and the diffusion prior jointly rather than sequentially. • Diffusing on the simplex or other statistical manifolds . These methods parameterize a categorical distribution over the vocabulary and diffuse its parameters directly, keeping the noise process on-manifold and avoiding a rounding step. SSD-LM ( Han et al., 2023 ) runs simplex diffusion in a semi-autoregressive block structure, Dirichlet diffusion ( Avdeyev et al., 2023 ) uses a Jacobi diffusion process on the probability simplex, and later variants ( Cheng et al., 2024 ; Davis et al., 2024 ; Jo and Hwang, 2025 ) extend the geometry to Fisher–Rao and Riemannian flow matching. • Reaching discrete data through dequantization or a Gaussian–discrete duality . Argmax flows ( Hoogeboom et al., 2021 ) lift categorical data into a continuous space via argmax-based variational dequantization, so continuous flows can be trained under a discrete likelihood; analog bits ( Chen et al., 2023 ) , BitLM ( Zhuang et al., 2026 ) , and CoBit ( Batzolis et al., 2026 ) instead map each token to a bitstring and diffuse from there; Duo ( Sahoo et al., 2025 ) establishes a duality between continuous Gaussian and uniform-state discrete diffusion, letting the two families share training and sampling machinery. Sigma sits in the token-embedding class, inheriting the learnable embedding and variational diffusion process of Plaid and RePlaid.

sections.heading: Scaling continuous dLMs to billions of parameters.
sections.text: Recent work pushes continuous dLMs into the billion-parameter regime, but along axes different from ours: for example, Cola-DLM ( Guo et al., 2026 ) ( ∼ \sim 2B, hierarchical latent-prior modeling), AURORA-LM ( Liang et al., 2026 ) (1B, flow matching over an autoencoded latent), and Categorical Flow Maps ( Davis et al., 2026 ) (1.7B, self-distilled for few-step generation). A separate line changes the base representation and scales through an existing LM backbone: BitLM ( Zhuang et al., 2026 ) places a bitwise diffusion head atop a causal LM up to 8B, TESS 2 ( Tae et al., 2025 ) adapts an autoregressive Mistral-7B into a generalist diffusion model with a simplex cross-entropy loss, and DSL-LLaDA ( Yu et al., 2026 ) scales continuous denoising via discrete stochastic localization ( Wu et al., 2026 ) on top of the LLaDA-8B masked-diffusion backbone ( Nie et al., 2025b ) . In contrast, Sigma is, to our knowledge, the first likelihood-trained continuous dLM at 3B/8B, and the first evaluated head-to-head with a matched masked dLM ( Fu et al., 2026 ) on conditional reasoning and code.

sections.heading: CFG in dLMs.
sections.text: Continuous dLMs realize the guidance condition in two ways. When there is no prompt (e.g., unconditional generation), several works repurpose the self-conditioning signal as the condition: ELF ( Hu et al., 2026 ) and AURORA-LM ( Liang et al., 2026 ) extrapolate between predictions made with and without the previous-step estimate. For conditional generation, DFM ( Potaptchik et al., 2026 ) , AURORA-LM ( Liang et al., 2026 ) , Cola-DLM ( Guo et al., 2026 ) , and BitLM ( Zhuang et al., 2026 ) extrapolate between a prompt-conditioned and an unconditional prediction, as in image diffusion models. A cost for this is that enabling it requires dropping the prompt context during training. FLM ( Lee et al., 2026 ) also leverages autoguidance ( Karras et al., 2024 ) for prediction sharpening. For discrete dLMs, LLaDA ( Nie et al., 2025b ) popularized an “unsupervised” CFG that runs one forward with full prompt and one with the prompt masked, then linearly extrapolates the two logit vectors before renormalizing; this has since been refined by more general discrete guidance mechanisms ( Schiff et al., 2025 ; Nisonoff et al., 2025 ) . Our steering ( Sec. 4.2 ) differs on three points: ( i ) the guidance condition is the clean prefix itself, and the unconditional branch simply drops that prefix so the noisy block attends only within itself; ( ii ) the extrapolation acts on the predicted clean embedding (equivalently the score), not on logits; ( iii ) it is a pure inference-time operation that requires no train-time dropout because sequence packing leaves the first block without context.

sections.heading: Autoregressive and block video diffusion.
sections.text: Our block-causal factorization (i.e., autoregressive across blocks, bidirectional Gaussian denoising within a block over a KV-cacheable clean prefix) closely mirrors recent video generation models that couple causal structure across frames with denoising within them ( Chen et al., 2024 ; Yin et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2025 ) . The bidirectional video-diffusion lineage ( Ho et al., 2022 ) was the original target of this conversion, and the autoregressive arm of Cosmos ( Agarwal et al., 2025 ) likewise structures video generation causally across frames. Diffusion Forcing ( Chen et al., 2024 ) trains a causal model with independent per-frame noise levels, unifying next-token prediction with full-sequence diffusion and enabling stable rollouts past the training horizon. CausVid ( Yin et al., 2025 ) and Self Forcing ( Huang et al., 2025 ) convert bidirectional video diffusion into causal, KV-cached autoregressive generators for fast streaming synthesis while curbing error accumulation along the rollout. These works share our central design tension (i.e., coupling causal, autoregressive structure with within-block diffusion) and several of their techniques (per-block noise schedules, rolling KV caches, distribution-matching distillation) transfer naturally to the language setting.

sections.heading: Appendix B Limitations and Future Work
sections.text: [Back to Sec. 7 in the main paper.] Despite the promising performance of continuous dLMs for language reasoning, several limitations remain. In this section, we outline these key challenges alongside promising directions for future research.

sections.heading: Inference Speed and Few-Step Trajectory Distillation.
sections.text: Continuous dLM decoding remains slower per generated token at high step counts compared to fully optimized autoregressive baselines. Under low step budgets, DDIM-4/8 exhibits a major performance drop relative to DDPM-256 ( Tab. 1 ). We observe that neither higher-order ODE solvers ( Sec. G.7 ) nor commit-stride sampling ( Sec. G.5 ) fully bridge this gap. To address this, we explore preliminary on-policy and off-policy Parallel Decoding Distillation (PDD), observing encouraging performance gains. Significant headroom remains in optimizing PDD head parameterizations, training objectives, and policy learning strategies. Given that standard DDIM sampling with 16 NFEs maintains decent performance, effective distillation holds substantial potential for 4 × 4\times – 8 × 8\times acceleration, leveraging insights from continuous trajectory distillation in visual domains. Beyond PDD, extending trajectory distillation to consistency and flow-matching frameworks provides a promising path toward real-time continuous dLM generation. Finally, since our model involves self-conditioning, how to distill it into the few-step generative model remains an open question.

sections.heading: Encoder–Decoder Robustness.
sections.text: We observe that diffusion-based ELBO training tends to collapse the continuous embedding geometry because the readout decoder (the linear logit projection) is trained predominantly to reconstruct clean, final-step token embeddings. Consequently, the decoder becomes hypersensitive to subtle continuous perturbations. This sensitivity becomes severe when latent representations fall out-of-distribution (OOD), which occurs frequently during early denoising stages, low-NFE sampling, trajectory distillation, or aggressive score steering via CFG and ST ( Fig. 15 ). This latent-to-discrete mismatch might induce decoding errors that bottleneck reasoning performance, especially in code generation where a single syntax error yields complete benchmark failure. To mitigate embedding collapse and strengthen decoder robustness, future research could explore auxiliary cross-entropy losses evaluated across all diffusion timesteps or robustify the readout decoder via VAE-style pre-training prior to diffusion alignment.

sections.heading: Memory Overhead and Blockwise KV-Caching Dynamics.
sections.text: Operating blockwise continuous diffusion requires evaluating the transformer denoiser across N N reverse steps per continuous block. Although blockwise generation offers parallel decoding potential, repeatedly updating and querying key-value (KV) states across intermediate noise timesteps increases peak memory bandwidth demand compared to standard single-pass autoregressive KV-caching. Optimizing persistent KV-cache management, state-reuse across intermediate diffusion steps, and extending blockwise continuous diffusion to ultra-long context windows ( > 32 ​ k >32\text{k} tokens) remain important systems challenges for future hardware deployments.

sections.heading: Reward-Driven Inference-Time Scaling and Post-Training.
sections.text: Both inference-time reward steering and reward-driven post-training remain largely unexplored for continuous dLMs. At inference, our CFG + ST framework extends naturally to reward-model guidance, sequential Monte Carlo over the denoising SDE, and tilted sampling toward verifier-preferred regions. For post-training, continuous dLMs can in principle inherit the RL toolbox developed for image and video diffusion; whether it transfers from perceptual rewards to language verifiers (math checkers, unit tests, preference models) is an open direction.

sections.heading: Multimodal Reasoning and Unified Latents.
sections.text: Because the probability-flow ODE is natively well-defined in our continuous formulation, standard continuous image-diffusion techniques such as trajectory matching ( Song et al., 2023 ; Geng et al., 2025 ; Sabour et al., 2025 ; Boffi et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026a ; Shaul et al., 2026 ) and distribution matching ( Yin et al., 2024 ) can be directly imported into language modeling. Continuous diffusion is a natural fit for unified multimodal generation architectures ( Zhou et al., 2025 ; Xie et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2025 ) that bridge text with images, video, or audio. Extending Sigma to joint multimodal continuous trajectories presents a compelling path forward.

sections.heading: Confidence-based (greedy) sampling.
sections.text: Ancestral sampling with a large vocabulary and few steps often commits low-probability tokens early and cannot revisit them. Confidence-based samplers ( Chang et al., 2022 ; Nie et al., 2025b ; Ye et al., 2025 ; Fu et al., 2026 ) choose which positions to unmask by predicted confidence, and a temperature T ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] T\in[0,1] (typically zero, i.e., deterministic argmax decoding) when sampling from the categorical distribution. Two variants are commonly used: • Top- k k per step. Fix a budget k i k_{i} at step i i so that their sum is the sequence length. At step i i , commit the k i k_{i} masked positions with the highest confidence c l := ‖ 𝐱 θ l ​ ( 𝐳 t i ) ‖ ∞ c^{l}:=\|{\mathbf{x}}_{\theta}^{l}({\mathbf{z}}_{t_{i}})\|_{\infty} , and sample these positions from the probability distribution 𝐱 θ l ​ ( 𝐳 t i ) {\mathbf{x}}_{\theta}^{l}({\mathbf{z}}_{t_{i}}) with temperature T T . When T = 0 T=0 , this is the default sampler of LLaDA ( Nie et al., 2025b ) and Dream ( Ye et al., 2025 ) . The LLaDA and Dream baselines reported in Tabs. 2 and 4 are generated with k 1 = … = k L = 1 k_{1}=...=k_{L}=1 (i.e., unmasking one position at a time with the highest confidence). • Threshold per step. Fix a confidence threshold ϑ ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) \vartheta\in(0,1) . At step i i , commit every masked position with c l ≥ ϑ c^{l}\geq\vartheta , and sample these positions from the probability distribution 𝐱 θ l ​ ( 𝐳 t i ) {\mathbf{x}}_{\theta}^{l}({\mathbf{z}}_{t_{i}}) with temperature T T . When T = 0 T=0 , this is the greedy sampler of Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion ( Fu et al., 2026 ) and defines our masked baseline in Tabs. 1 , 3 , 2 and 4 using ϑ ∈ { 0.8 , 0.9 } \vartheta\in\{0.8,0.9\} as the threshold. Like ancestral sampling, these samplers preserve the absorbing property that an unmasked token stays fixed for the rest of the trajectory.

sections.heading: Scaling.
sections.text: Following the scaling study of masked dLM on text by Nie et al. (2025a) , the field has scaled along two lines. The from-scratch line trains a masked dLM directly on raw data: LLaDA-8B ( Nie et al., 2025b ) rivals AR models of the same size, and LLaDA-MoE ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) pushes the objective into a sparse mixture-of-experts backbone at 1.4B active parameters. The LLaDA-8B backbone has been further extended along orthogonal axes without additional pre-training scaling: LLaDA 1.5 ( Zhu et al., 2026a ) adds variance-reduced preference alignment and LLaDA-V ( You et al., 2026 ) adds visual instruction tuning. The AR-adaptation line instead starts from a pretrained AR checkpoint and performances continual pre-training to turn it into a masked dLM. Dream-7B ( Ye et al., 2025 ) converts Qwen2.5-7B into a masked dLM via the DiffuLLaMA shift-operation trick ( Gong et al., 2025 ) . The remainder of this line instead converts the AR checkpoint into a blockwise masked dLM ( Arriola et al., 2025 ) that preserves KV caching across blocks, a conversion far cheaper than pre-training from scratch: Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion ( Fu et al., 2026 ) , FLARE ( Zhu et al., 2026b ) , SDAR ( Cheng et al., 2026 ) at 1.7 ∼ \sim 30B (including a 30B MoE), and most recently LLaDA 2.0-mini/flash ( Bie et al., 2025 ) at 16B and 100B (MoE), the largest open masked dLM to date. Closed-source frontier deployments such as Mercury ( Inception Labs et al., 2025 ) and Seed Diffusion ( Song et al., 2025 ) also fall into this block masked dLM paradigm.

sections.heading: Appendix E Implementation Details and Additional Results for Pre-training
sections.text: [Back to Sec. 3.2 in the main paper.]

sections.heading: Architecture.
sections.text: Following NLD ( Fu et al., 2026 ) , we adopt the transformer architecture of Ministral ( Liu et al., 2026a ) : • 3B: 26 layers, width 3072, FFN 9216, 32 query and 8 key/value heads (head dimension 128), SwiGLU, RMSNorm, YaRN-scaled rotary embeddings ( θ = 10 6 \theta=10^{6} ), and untied embeddings. This adds up to 3.0B non-embedding and 3.8B total parameters. • 8B: 34 layers, width 4096, FFN 14336, same 32 query and 8 key/value heads (head dimension 128) and same SwiGLU, RMSNorm, YaRN rotary embeddings and untied embeddings. This adds up to 7.4B non-embedding and 8.5B total parameters.

sections.heading: Optimization.
sections.text: For γ ~ \tilde{\gamma} and 𝐄 {\mathbf{E}} , we use AdamW with β 1 = 0.9 \beta_{1}=0.9 , β 2 = 0.95 \beta_{2}=0.95 , no weight decay (rows of 𝐄 {\mathbf{E}} unit-norm), and peak learning rate η peak = 1 × 10 − 2 \eta_{\text{peak}}=1\times 10^{-2} ; γ 0 , γ 1 \gamma_{0},\gamma_{1} use the same setting but with weight decay 0.1 0.1 ( Yang et al., 2026 ) . For other parameters, we follow NLD and use AdamW with β 1 = 0.9 \beta_{1}=0.9 , β 2 = 0.95 \beta_{2}=0.95 , weight decay 0.1 0.1 , and η peak = 1 × 10 − 5 \eta_{\text{peak}}=1\times 10^{-5} . For all parameters, we use gradient clipping value 1.0 1.0 . The learning rate schedule is Warmup-Stable-Decay over 150K steps: 1 % 1\% linear warmup to η peak \eta_{\text{peak}} , constant through step 120K, then exponential decay to 10 % 10\% of η peak \eta_{\text{peak}} .

sections.heading: Self-conditioning (SC).
sections.text: SC injects the model’s own detached clean-embedding prediction into the projected noised input stream with a bias-free, zero-initialized linear layer mapping ℝ d e \mathbb{R}^{d_{e}} to the hidden width ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} : a first pass with 𝐞 sc = 𝟎 {\mathbf{e}}_{\text{sc}}={\mathbf{0}} , then a second pass with d e ​ sg ⁡ ( 𝐞 sc ) \sqrt{d_{e}}\,\operatorname{sg}({\mathbf{e}}_{\text{sc}}) through that linear layer.

sections.heading: Time conditioning.
sections.text: For diffusion stream, a single γ \gamma is sampled per block and shared across its tokens. We encode γ \gamma using fixed sinusoidal features with frequencies exp ⁡ ( linspace ⁡ ( − 5 , 5 , 32 ) ) \exp(\mathrm{linspace}(-5,5,32)) , concatenating [ sin , cos ] [\sin,\cos] into 64 dimensions. A bias-free, zero-initialized linear layer projects this encoding to the hidden width, where it is added to the projected noised input.

sections.heading: Numerical precision.
sections.text: All parameters are stored in BF16 , and the transformer also computes in BF16 through the forward and backward pass, its linear logit heads included; gradient accumulation and the data-parallel all-reduce run in FP32 . The small modules outside the transformer upcast their weights at use. Among these, most computes in FP32 : the diffusion embeddings and their Gaussian corruption and up-projection, the sinusoidal γ \gamma features and their up-projection, and the SC up-projection. The noise schedule computes in FP64 , covering the endpoints γ 0 , γ 1 \gamma_{0},\gamma_{1} , the minus log-SNR γ \gamma and its derivative, and the α t , σ t \alpha_{t},\sigma_{t} derived from them. These drop FP64 at three points: γ \gamma before the sinusoidal features, α t , σ t \alpha_{t},\sigma_{t} at the corruption, and the variance rescaling before the up-projection for 𝐳 t {\mathbf{z}}_{t} . These modules incur negligible FLOPs, so the extra precision is a cheap precaution followed from Gulrajani and Hashimoto (2023) ; Yang et al. (2026) . The optimizer keeps FP32 master weights and Adam moments, sharded across data-parallel ranks (distributed optimizer).

sections.heading: AR regularization.
sections.text: We searched over w diff ∈ { 0.3 , 1.0 } w_{\text{diff}}\in\{0.3,1.0\} . Interestingly, when w diff = 1.0 w_{\text{diff}}=1.0 , adding the AR regularization even improved diffusion PPL ( Fig. 3(c) ). However, we found that switching to w diff = 0.3 w_{\text{diff}}=0.3 at 200B tokens offers the best convergence for both losses ( Fig. 3(c) ); this is our flagship 3B Sigma model which we evaluate in subsequent sections. We also trained our 8B Sigma model using this configuration.

sections.heading: Benchmarks.
sections.text: We evaluate on ARC-e/c ( Clark et al., 2018 ) , HellaSwag ( Zellers et al., 2019 ) , PIQA ( Bisk et al., 2020 ) , WinoGrande ( Sakaguchi et al., 2020 ) , and MMLU ( Hendrycks et al., 2021 ) . Per Open LLM Leaderboard convention we report acc_norm (normalized by character length) on the four length-varying 0-shot tasks and plain acc on WinoGrande and MMLU. These benchmarks score a candidate response 𝐫 {\mathbf{r}} against a prompt 𝐩 {\mathbf{p}} by comparing log ⁡ p θ ​ ( 𝐫 ∣ 𝐩 ) \log p_{\theta}({\mathbf{r}}\mid{\mathbf{p}}) across candidates.

sections.heading: Scoring our continuous method.
sections.text: Sigma does not give likelihood in closed form, but a surrogate based on the NELBO: taking the prompt as the clean prefix and the candidate as the block to be denoised, and then applying 4 verbatim with 𝐩 {\mathbf{p}} as 𝐱 ( < b ) {\mathbf{x}}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}<b})} and 𝐫 {\mathbf{r}} as 𝐱 ( b ) {\mathbf{x}}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})} : − log ⁡ p θ ​ ( 𝐫 ∣ 𝐩 ) ≤ ℒ NELBO ​ ( 𝐫 , 𝐩 ) \displaystyle-\log p_{\theta}({\mathbf{r}}\mid{\mathbf{p}})\leq\mathcal{L}_{\text{NELBO}}({\mathbf{r}};{\mathbf{p}}) = KL ( q ( 𝐳 1 ∣ 𝐫 ) ∥ p ( 𝐳 1 ) ) + 𝔼 q ⁡ ( 𝐳 0 ∣ 𝐫 ) [ ∑ l = 1 | 𝐫 | − log ⟨ 𝐱 θ l ( 𝐳 0 , 0 ; 𝐩 ) , 𝐫 l ⟩ ] \displaystyle=\operatorname{KL}(q({\mathbf{z}}_{1}\mid{\mathbf{r}})\,\|\,p({\mathbf{z}}_{1}))+\E_{q({\mathbf{z}}_{0}\mid{\mathbf{r}})}\big[{\textstyle\sum}_{l=1}^{|{\mathbf{r}}|}-\log\langle{\mathbf{x}}_{\theta}^{l}({\mathbf{z}}_{0},0;{\mathbf{p}}),{\mathbf{r}}^{l}\rangle\big] − 1 2 ​ 𝔼 t ∼ Unif ⁡ [ 0 , 1 ] ​ 𝔼 q ⁡ ( 𝐳 t ∣ 𝐫 ) ​ [ SNR ′ ⁡ ( t ) ​ ‖ 𝐞 θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , 𝐩 ) − 𝐞 ‖ 2 ] . \displaystyle-\tfrac{1}{2}\ \E_{t\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,1]}\E_{q({\mathbf{z}}_{t}\mid{\mathbf{r}})}[\operatorname{SNR}^{\prime}(t)\|{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{z}}_{t},t;{\mathbf{p}})-{\mathbf{e}}\|^{2}]. (17) In practice, we evaluate 17 with 128 128 stratified samples t k = k + u 128 t_{k}=\frac{k+u}{128} , k = 0 , … , 127 k=0,\dots,127 , u ∼ Unif ⁡ [ 0 , 1 ] u\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,1] and 8 8 reconstruction samples.

sections.heading: Scoring the masked baseline via count-based NELBO.
sections.text: Here we use the notation for masked diffusion defined in App. C . Let 𝐩 {\mathbf{p}} be the prompt and 𝐫 {\mathbf{r}} be a candidate response. We generate the masked states by the mask set , instead of randomly masking each position with probability t t : for M ⊆ { 1 , … , L 𝐫 } M\subseteq\{1,\dots,L_{\mathbf{r}}\} , where L 𝐫 := | 𝐫 | L_{\mathbf{r}}:=|{\mathbf{r}}| , we obtain 𝐳 M {\mathbf{z}}_{M} from masking indices in M M of 𝐫 {\mathbf{r}} , and denote C ( M ) := ∑ l ∈ M − log ⟨ 𝐱 θ l ( 𝐳 M ; 𝐩 ) , 𝐫 l ⟩ C(M):=\sum_{l\in M}-\log\langle{\mathbf{x}}_{\theta}^{l}({\mathbf{z}}_{M};{\mathbf{p}}),\,{\mathbf{r}}^{l}\rangle their cross entropy. Under α t = 1 − t \alpha_{t}=1-t , 9 gives the continuous-time bound; integrating t t out yields an average over the number of masked tokens ( Ou et al., 2025 ; Nie et al., 2025b ) : − log ⁡ p θ ​ ( 𝐫 ∣ 𝐩 ) ≤ ℒ MDLM ​ ( 𝐫 , 𝐩 ) \displaystyle-\log p_{\theta}({\mathbf{r}}\mid{\mathbf{p}})\;\leq\;\mathcal{L}_{\text{MDLM}}({\mathbf{r}};{\mathbf{p}}) = 𝔼 t ∼ Unif ⁡ [ 0 , 1 ] ⁡ [ 1 t ​ 𝔼 M ∼ Bern ​ ( t ) ⊗ L 𝐫 ⁡ C ⁡ ( M ) ] \displaystyle\;=\;\E_{t\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,1]}\Big[\frac{1}{t}\,\E_{M\sim\mathrm{Bern}(t)^{\otimes L_{\mathbf{r}}}}C(M)\Big] (18) = 𝔼 n ∼ Unif ⁡ { 1 , … , L 𝐫 } ⁡ [ L 𝐫 n ​ 𝔼 M ∼ Unif ⁡ ( [ L 𝐫 ] n ) ⁡ C ⁡ ( M ) ] , \displaystyle\;=\;\E_{n\sim\operatorname{Unif}\{1,\ldots,L_{\mathbf{r}}\}}\Big[\frac{L_{\mathbf{r}}}{n}\,\E_{M\sim\operatorname{Unif}\binom{[L_{\mathbf{r}}]}{n}}C(M)\Big], (19) where ( [ L 𝐫 ] n ) \binom{[L_{\mathbf{r}}]}{n} means the set of all n n -element subsets of [ L 𝐫 ] := { 1 , 2 , … , L 𝐫 } [L_{\mathbf{r}}]:=\{1,2,...,L_{\mathbf{r}}\} . 19 is a Rao–Blackwellized low-variance estimator of 18 , manifested in the following three major differences: (i) The 1 t \frac{1}{t} weight becomes L 𝐫 n ≤ L 𝐫 \frac{L_{\mathbf{r}}}{n}\leq L_{\mathbf{r}} , so rare small- t t draws that leave one or two masked tokens would not cause the variance of the estimator to blow up. (ii) Bernoulli masking leaves 𝐫 {\mathbf{r}} wholly unmasked with probability ( 1 − t ) L 𝐫 (1-t)^{L_{\mathbf{r}}} , which may be common for short responses and wastes a forward pass, while the n ≥ 1 n\geq 1 constraint avoids this. (iii) As n n is finite, we can similarly use stratified sampling as the t t -grid above, spreading counts evenly over { 1 , … , L 𝐫 } \{1,\ldots,L_{\mathbf{r}}\} from one uniform offset, so every batch covers all masking rates. In practice, we use 19 with 128 128 low-discrepancy draws n k n_{k} and standard random sampling for M k M_{k} for Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion ( Fu et al., 2026 ) in Tabs. 6 and 7 . On MMLU candidates are single tokens, so L 𝐫 = n = 1 L_{\mathbf{r}}=n=1 and 19 is exact after one forward pass, while 18 would still be averaging 1 t \frac{1}{t} . We found 19 to work better than 18 in early experiments.

sections.heading: Length generalization.
sections.text: Diffusion training denoises blocks of exactly L ′ L^{\prime} tokens from packed sequences of length L L , whereas candidates are typically short and occasionally longer than L ′ L^{\prime} . For each ( 𝐩 , 𝐫 ) ({\mathbf{p}},{\mathbf{r}}) pair, we apply causal attention over 𝐩 {\mathbf{p}} and bidirectional attention over 𝐫 {\mathbf{r}} , assuming that the bidirectional attention can generalize to response length other than L ′ L^{\prime} . The attention map follows the conditional branch in Fig. 4(a) .

sections.heading: G.1 Reasoning and Coding Benchmark Setup
sections.text: [Back to Secs. 4 and 5 in the main paper.] We describe the harness, scoring pipeline, and sampler that produce Tabs. 1 , 2 and 8 . The scoring pipeline is consistent for all base models and generation modes.

sections.heading: Benchmarks and few-shot budgets.
sections.text: We use six tasks from lm-evaluation-harness following Fu et al. (2026) : GSM8K (8-shot, 1319 questions) ( Cobbe et al., 2021 ) , Minerva Math (4-shot, 5000 questions 2 2 2 Number of questions in each sub-domain: algebra 1187, counting/prob 474, geometry 479, intermediate algebra 903, number theory 540, prealgebra 871, precalc 546. ) ( Lewkowycz et al., 2022 ) , HumanEval and HumanEval+ (0-shot, 164 questions) ( Chen et al., 2021 ) , and MBPP and MBPP+ (3-shot, 500 and 378 questions, respectively) ( Austin et al., 2021b ) . The per-task generation budget is 256 tokens for GSM8K and 512 tokens for the other five tasks.

sections.heading: Scoring.
sections.text: GSM8K is scored by exact-match on the numerical answer, extracted from the model’s response by a permissive regex that keeps the last number appearing in the completion (stripping separators and trailing punctuation). Minerva Math is scored by symbolic equivalence after canonicalizing boxed and inline expressions. HumanEval and HumanEval+ report post-processed pass@1: the completion is stripped out of the Markdown code fence, an AST-based longest-valid-code extraction is applied, and the resulting program is executed against the task test cases in the container. MBPP and MBPP+ report the harness pass@1 directly without this post-processing step, matching the convention of prior work.

sections.heading: Decoding configuration.
sections.text: Unless overridden in the corresponding row of Tab. 1 , all Sigma diffusion-mode runs use block size L ′ = 32 L^{\prime}=32 , BF16 model weights at inference time, argmax readout at the final diffusion step, and operation of SC follows Fig. 4(b) . The DDPM-256 row uses the ancestral sampler of DDPM on the EDM ρ = 7 \rho=7 schedule ( Sec. G.6 ); the DDIM-32 row uses the deterministic sampler of DDIM on the uniform- γ \gamma schedule; the row-specific guidance strength w w and score temperature τ \tau appear in the table caption. Commit stride is the block size unless otherwise specified.

sections.heading: Seed error bars.
sections.text: Each Sigma diffusion row aggregates 10 10 independent sampling lanes as follows. For question i i , we independently draw 10 10 responses under the same decoder with 10 10 different seeds. Let s i , j s_{i,j} be the score of the j j -th response to question i i . We first average over questions to obtain 10 10 per-lane scores s j = mean i ⁡ ( s i , j ) s_{j}=\operatorname{mean}_{i}(s_{i,j}) for j = 1 , … , 10 j=1,\dots,10 , and then obtain s ¯ = mean j ⁡ ( s j ) \bar{s}=\operatorname{mean}_{j}(s_{j}) together with the across-lane standard deviation σ ^ = std j ⁡ ( s j ) \hat{\sigma}=\operatorname{std}_{j}(s_{j}) . The half-widths in Tab. 1 are 2 10 ​ σ ^ \frac{2}{\sqrt{10}}\hat{\sigma} , an approximate 95 % 95\% confidence interval for the mean.

sections.heading: Baseline decoders.
sections.text: The AR-mode for NLD and Sigma row uses greedy argmax at each step; NLD’s diffusion-mode row uses the confidence-threshold greedy sampler of Fu et al. (2026) (block size L ′ = 32 L^{\prime}=32 ; argmax \argmax readout at every position whose top-1 probability exceeds a threshold; we report the better of thresholds 0.8 0.8 and 0.9 0.9 per task). For LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B we quote each model’s best diffusion-mode number without the confidence-threshold rule: at each denoising step the single position with the highest top-1 confidence is unmasked. We refer readers to App. C for details of inference algorithms for masked diffusion models.

sections.heading: G.2 Sweeping Classifier-Free Guidance and Score Temperature
sections.text: [Back to Sec. 4.2 or Sec. 4.3 in the main paper.] In Figs. 10 and 11 , we present the full tables for CFG and ST sweep for our Sigma -3B models trained with and without AR regularization, respectively. Figure 10 : Sweeping CFG and ST for Sigma -3B trained with AR regularization. Accuracies are averaged over 10 random seeds. Red : per-task best; orange : within 1 point of per-task best; green : best average across 6 tasks. For this model, per-task best and best average align on 5 out of 6 tasks. In the exception of Minerva Math (subset; random 10 % 10\% from each subtask), per-task best is still within 1 point from best average. We report best average ( CFG = 2 \text{CFG}=2 , ST = 0.1 \text{ST}=0.1 ) in Fig. 5 and Tab. 1 . Figure 11 : Sweeping CFG and ST for Sigma -3B trained without AR regularization. Accuracies are averaged over 10 random seeds. Red : per-task best; orange : within 1 point of per-task best; green : best average across 6 tasks. Both per-task best and best average are worse than Sigma -3B trained AR regularization ( Fig. 10 ).

sections.heading: G.3 Ablation Study: Steering in Logit Space Instead of Embedding Space
sections.text: [Back to Sec. 4.2 in the main paper.] Both steering knobs introduced in Sec. 4.2 act on the predicted clean embedding 𝐞 θ ∈ ℝ L ′ × d e {\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{L^{\prime}\times d_{e}} , equivalently on the score or velocity. Recall that our denoiser leverages categorical reparameterization , i.e., 𝐞 θ = softmax ⁡ ( ℓ θ ) ​ 𝐄 = 𝐱 θ ​ 𝐄 {\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}=\operatorname{softmax}({\bm{\ell}}_{\theta}){\mathbf{E}}={\mathbf{x}}_{\theta}{\mathbf{E}} , where ℓ θ ∈ ℝ L ′ × V {\bm{\ell}}_{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{L^{\prime}\times V} are the predicted logits, and softmax \operatorname{softmax} operates in the vocabulary dimension. Thus, a natural alternative is to apply the same operations to ℓ θ {\bm{\ell}}_{\theta} before the softmax \operatorname{softmax} . This is the form of guidance used by discrete dLMs, which does not have embedding-space prediction to steer ( Nie et al., 2025b ; Li et al., 2025 ; Schiff et al., 2025 ) ( App. A ).

sections.heading: Logit-space CFG (LCFG).
sections.text: Reusing the notations in Sec. G.4 , with the same fully unconditional bad prediction, we do softmax on the extrapolated logits: 𝐞 θ w , logit := softmax ⁡ ( ℓ θ ∅ , 𝟎 + w ⁡ [ ℓ θ + − ℓ θ ∅ , 𝟎 ] ) ​ 𝐄 , w ≥ 1 , \displaystyle{\mathbf{e}}^{w,\text{logit}}_{\theta}:=\operatorname{softmax}({\bm{\ell}}^{\varnothing,{\mathbf{0}}}_{\theta}+w\,[{\bm{\ell}}^{+}_{\theta}-{\bm{\ell}}^{\varnothing,{\mathbf{0}}}_{\theta}]){\mathbf{E}},\qquad w\geq 1, against our default 𝐞 θ w = 𝐞 θ ∅ , 𝟎 + w ⁡ [ 𝐞 θ + − 𝐞 θ ∅ , 𝟎 ] {\mathbf{e}}^{w}_{\theta}={\mathbf{e}}^{\varnothing,{\mathbf{0}}}_{\theta}+w[{\mathbf{e}}^{+}_{\theta}-{\mathbf{e}}^{\varnothing,{\mathbf{0}}}_{\theta}] of CFG , which extrapolates after the softmax. The two coincide at w = 1 w=1 (i.e., no guidance).

sections.heading: Logit temperature (LT).
sections.text: This is the analogue of ST in logit space, which rescales the conditional logits themselves: 𝐞 θ T := softmax ⁡ ( ℓ θ + T ) ​ 𝐄 , T ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] , \displaystyle{\mathbf{e}}^{T}_{\theta}:=\operatorname{softmax}\Big(\frac{{\bm{\ell}}^{+}_{\theta}}{T}\Big){\mathbf{E}},\qquad T\in[0,1], where T = 1 T=1 recovers the conditional mean embedding prediction (i.e., no guidance), and smaller T T sharpens. The T → 0 T\to 0 limit is the maximum a posteriori (MAP) denoiser 𝐞 θ 0 = 𝐄 ⁡ [ argmax ℓ θ + ] {\mathbf{e}}^{0}_{\theta}={\mathbf{E}}[\argmax{\bm{\ell}}^{+}_{\theta}] , which snaps the prediction onto a single vocabulary embedding. We remark that both operations change the trajectory only; tokens are still read out as the argmax \argmax of the conditional logits at the final step t = 0 t=0 , exactly as in Secs. 4.1 and 2 . Also, LCFG does not cost extra compute compared with the embedding-space counterpart, since we need to get both conditional and unconditional logit predictions.

sections.heading: LCFG peaks early and tops out lower.
sections.text: Tab. 9 shows that LCFG peaks at w = 2 w=2 in all four settings and then declines monotonically, while embedding-space CFG keeps improving out to w = 4 ∼ 10 w=4\sim 10 . Comparing each at its own optimum, logit space gives a marginal gain of + 0.30 +0.30 on GSM8K/DDIM but loses by 5.68 5.68 , 2.44 2.44 , and 17.26 17.26 points in the other three settings.

sections.heading: Logit temperature sharpens effectively, and the MAP denoiser does not collapse.
sections.text: Tab. 10 shows sharpening alone is worth a great deal on DDPM, lifting GSM8K from 52.44 52.44 at T = 1 T=1 to 79.11 79.11 at T = 1 5 T=\frac{1}{5} . The curve then stays flat all the way to the hard endpoint: the entire range from T = 1 3 T=\frac{1}{3} to T = 0 T=0 spans only 0.5 0.5 points, and T = 0 T=0 itself scores 78.61 78.61 . Committing by argmax \argmax at high noise therefore costs nothing measurable here, and the on-manifold denoiser is a viable operating point rather than a degenerate one.

sections.heading: What logit-space guidance adds over sharpening is neutral at best.
sections.text: Note that if the unconditional branch predicted zero (i.e., a uniform distribution over the vocabulary), logit CFG at weight w w will be equivalent to logit temperature at T = 1 w T=\frac{1}{w} . The gap between the two therefore measures the contribution of the structured part of the unconditional logits, which is the entire content of logit-space guidance. The bottom rows of Tab. 10 show that contribution is negligible at w = 2 w=2 and then strictly harmful at larger w w . So logit-space CFG is best understood as a more expensive but still poorly behaved sharpener.

sections.heading: Logit temperature composes with ST, but adds nothing on top of CFG.
sections.text: LT and ST sharpen different objects: LT tempers the categorical posterior and then takes its mean, so its prediction stays inside the convex hull of 𝐄 {\mathbf{E}} and saturates at the MAP vertex, whereas ST extrapolates the mean prediction away from 𝐳 t α t \frac{{\mathbf{z}}_{t}}{\alpha_{t}} and can go outside the unit ball. Tab. 11 confirms they do compose: on DDIM, where ST = 0.3 =0.3 is already active, adding LT at T = 1 2 T=\frac{1}{2} lifts GSM8K for 9.42 9.42 points that score temperature alone does not reach. However, when CFG and ST are already on, adding a third sharpener LT harms accuracy.

sections.heading: Conclusion.
sections.text: Logit-space steering does sharpen, and logit temperature in particular is a simple knob requiring no second branch as in Fig. 4(a) . However, it does not outperform the default embedding-space CFG in general. We therefore keep the embedding-space formulation of CFG and ST throughout.

sections.heading: G.4 Ablation Study: Choosing the Bad Prediction for CFG with Self-conditioning
sections.text: [Back to Sec. 4.2 in the main paper.] Standard CFG ( Ho and Salimans, 2022 ) , also following the idea of auto-guidance ( Karras et al., 2024 ) , extrapolates a conditional prediction away from a “bad” prediction to sharpen the model’s prediction. Self-conditioning introduces a second source of conditioning, as is used in existing continuous dLMs (e.g., Lee et al. (2026) ; Potaptchik et al. (2026) ; Hu et al. (2026) ; see App. A for detailed discussion). We define the following notations in this subsection: 𝐞 θ + \displaystyle{\mathbf{e}}^{+}_{\theta} : = 𝐞 θ ​ ( 𝐳 t ( b ) , t , 𝐜 , 𝐞 sc ) , \displaystyle:={\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})},t;{\mathbf{c}},{\mathbf{e}}_{\text{sc}}), 𝐞 θ 𝐜 , 𝟎 \displaystyle{\mathbf{e}}^{{\mathbf{c}},{\mathbf{0}}}_{\theta} : = 𝐞 θ ​ ( 𝐳 t ( b ) , t , 𝐜 , 𝟎 ) , \displaystyle:={\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})},t;{\mathbf{c}},{\mathbf{0}}), 𝐞 θ ∅ , 𝟎 \displaystyle{\mathbf{e}}^{\varnothing,{\mathbf{0}}}_{\theta} : = 𝐞 θ ​ ( 𝐳 t ( b ) , t , ∅ , 𝟎 ) , \displaystyle:={\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})},t;\varnothing,{\mathbf{0}}), where the good prediction 𝐞 θ + {\mathbf{e}}^{+}_{\theta} is the conditional prediction that uses both the clean context and SC; for either bad prediction 𝐞 θ − ∈ { 𝐞 θ 𝐜 , 𝟎 , 𝐞 θ ∅ , 𝟎 } {\mathbf{e}}^{-}_{\theta}\in\{{\mathbf{e}}^{{\mathbf{c}},{\mathbf{0}}}_{\theta},{\mathbf{e}}^{\varnothing,{\mathbf{0}}}_{\theta}\} , the guided mean embedding prediction is 𝐞 θ w = 𝐞 θ + + ( w − 1 ) ​ ( 𝐞 θ + − 𝐞 θ − ) . \displaystyle{\mathbf{e}}^{w}_{\theta}={\mathbf{e}}^{+}_{\theta}+(w-1)({\mathbf{e}}^{+}_{\theta}-{\mathbf{e}}^{-}_{\theta}). The context-preserving baseline keeps the prompt and previously generated blocks in both branches and sets 𝐞 θ − ← 𝐞 θ 𝐜 , 𝟎 {\mathbf{e}}^{-}_{\theta}\leftarrow{\mathbf{e}}^{{\mathbf{c}},{\mathbf{0}}}_{\theta} ; it therefore extrapolates only away from the prediction made without SC. Our proposed method in Sec. 4.2 instead uses the fully unconditional branch 𝐞 θ − ← 𝐞 θ ∅ , 𝟎 {\mathbf{e}}^{-}_{\theta}\leftarrow{\mathbf{e}}^{\varnothing,{\mathbf{0}}}_{\theta} , removing both clean context and SC.

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: As shown in Tabs. 12 and 13 , the fully unconditional bad prediction (ours) is consistently stronger in the useful guidance range: it almost wins every matched CFG weight in sweep on both tasks and both samplers, and, tuned over the sweep, reaches a higher ceiling in each task. Thus, we conclude that the advantage shown here is not an artifact of using different guidance search ranges.

sections.heading: G.5 Ablation Study: Commit-Stride Sampling
sections.text: [Back to Sec. 4 in the main paper.] Beyond blockwise decoding of L ′ L^{\prime} tokens per denoising window, we further introduce a commit stride S ∈ { 1 , … , L ′ } S\in\{1,\dots,L^{\prime}\} . Each denoising window still runs the same blockwise reverse process over a block of fresh Gaussian noise with length L ′ = 32 L^{\prime}=32 , but only the leading S ∈ { 8 , 16 , 32 } S\in\{8,16,32\} tokens are committed back into the causal KV cache; the remaining L ′ − S L^{\prime}-S tail positions are discarded and re-drawn as fresh noise in the next window (which is shifted forward by S S absolute positions). Setting S ← L ′ S\leftarrow L^{\prime} recovers the default block-decoding method. The pseudocode for commit stride can be found in Alg. 2 . This is a pure inference-time technique that further improves the output quality even under matched compute budgets, as we will see below.

sections.heading: Setup.
sections.text: We evaluate on the base models of Tabs. 1 and 2 : Sigma -3B and Sigma -8B, both with block size L ′ = 32 L^{\prime}=32 . Decoding invariants match the diffusion-mode rows of Tab. 1 . For each stride, CFG weight w w and ST τ \tau are chosen based on the number of DDIM steps per window: ( w , τ ) = ( 3 , 0.2 ) (w,\tau)=(3,0.2) at ≥ 64 \geq 64 steps, ( 3 , 0.3 ) (3,0.3) at 32 32 steps, ( 3 , 0.5 ) (3,0.5) at 16 16 steps, and ( 3 , 0.8 ) (3,0.8) at 8 8 steps, following the recommendation in Fig. 14 . All cells generate 10 10 samples for each prompt and report mean ± \pm two standard errors ( Sec. G.1 ).

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: Tab. 16 shows that none of these higher-order updates improves accuracy over DDIM at the tested low-NFE sampling settings. The closest alternative is ρ \rho AB1-DEIS at 8 8 steps, but it still trails DDIM on GSM8K and HumanEval and is much worse on MBPP. Increasing the budget from 8 8 to 16 16 steps improves DDIM on every task, while the higher-order solvers do not improve reliably. ρ \rho AB2-DEIS and ρ \rho RK-DEIS become especially unstable at 16 16 steps.

sections.heading: Trajectory diagnosis.
sections.text: We perform a trajectory diagnosis by running different solvers from the same initial Gaussian noise 𝐳 1 {\mathbf{z}}_{1} given the same prompt and few-shot examples, saving the complete block- 0 0 trajectory. We use the first 32 32 questions of either GSM8K or HumanEval dataset, draw eight generations per question, and use three CFG–ST configurations ( w , τ ) ∈ { ( 3 , 0.4 ) , ( 3 , 0.6 ) , ( 2 , 0.7 ) } (w,\tau)\in\{(3,0.4),(3,0.6),(2,0.7)\} , each with self-conditioning on and off. This gives 2 2 tasks × \times 3 3 CFG–ST pairs × \times 2 2 self-conditioning configurations = 12 =12 settings. For each setting, the initial eight-lane noise tensor is identical across solvers and step budgets. We evaluate runs with 8 , 16 , 32 , 64 , 128 , 8,16,32,64,128, and 256 256 sampling steps together with a paired DDIM- 512 512 high-resolution reference as ground truth. Recall that all embedding vectors in 𝐄 {\mathbf{E}} are unit-norm, and thus ideally our terminal state 𝐳 0 {\mathbf{z}}_{0} should be close to the unit sphere. Panels (a) and (b) of Fig. 15 measure the geometry of the terminal latent states. Panel (a) averages | ‖ 𝐳 0 ‖ − 1 | |\|{\mathbf{z}}_{0}\|-1| within each setting and then equally across the 12 12 settings. For panel (b), we compute the nearest-embedding cosine similarity max k ⁡ cos ⁡ ( 𝐳 0 , 𝐄 k ) \max_{k}\cos({\mathbf{z}}_{0},{\mathbf{E}}_{k}) , take its fifth percentile within each setting, and then average the 12 12 setting-level percentiles. This tail statistic reveals endpoints stranded between vocabulary vertices. Error bars are standard errors across settings. At 8 8 steps, the mean off-sphere distance is 0.014 0.014 for DDIM, but 1.29 1.29 for ρ \rho AB1-DEIS and 26.2 26.2 for DPM-Solver++(2M); their fifth-percentile nearest-embedding cosine is 0.994 0.994 , 0.851 0.851 , and 0.845 0.845 , respectively. Thus, coarse higher-order extrapolation can move 𝐳 0 {\mathbf{z}}_{0} far outside the clean embedding manifold. Because the reconstruction term is applied only at t = 0 t=0 4 , the model is not trained to decode such off-manifold terminal states, this causes a large decoding error. By 32 32 steps, all three methods return close to the sphere and to a vocabulary vertex. Figure 15 : Endpoint geometry under low-step ODE solvers. (a) Terminal distance from the unit-sphere vocabulary manifold. (b) Fifth-percentile cosine similarity to the nearest vocabulary embedding. At 8 8 steps, higher-order extrapolation leaves endpoints far off-manifold and between vocabulary vertices, whereas these differences largely disappear by 32 32 steps.

sections.heading: Implications and future work.
sections.text: This negative result suggests that low-NFE inference for Sigma is not limited only by the formal order of the ODE integrator. Under strong CFG, ST, and SC, the effective denoising field can be less smooth than the trajectories for which standard image-diffusion solvers were designed. In this regime, formal integration order alone is not a reliable predictor of downstream quality, and DDIM remains the most robust choice among the solvers tested. We leave exploration of more stable and efficient higher-order ODE solvers for future work.

sections.heading: G.8 Pass@ k k Evaluation
sections.text: [Back to Tab. 2 in the main paper.] We study inference-time scaling in two distinct evaluation regimes. First, we compare the pretrained 3B models on MBPP, Minerva Geometry, and GSM8K under few-shot prompting. Second, we compare the instruct 3B models on AIME 2025 under the non-thinking protocol of Tab. 3 .

sections.heading: Metric.
sections.text: For a problem with c c correct answers among n n generations, we use the standard unbiased estimator pass@ ​ k = 1 − ( n − c k ) ( n k ) \text{pass@}k=1-\frac{\binom{n-c}{k}}{\binom{n}{k}} and average it over problems to obtain the pass@ k k accuracy on a evaluation dataset. Cross-family uncertainty is computed from paired per-problem differences and reported as a 95 % 95\% confidence interval.

Because the tested grids differ in size, this is a best-of-grid comparison; the right panel provides the complementary fixed-configuration result. One fixed Sigma configuration reaches the same pass@256 value of 0.918 0.918 , compared with 0.876 0.876 for NLD.

sections.heading: String-diversity diagnostic.
sections.text: We further investigate exact-string repetition as a partial proxy for output diversity, after stripping leading and trailing whitespaces. At the selected fixed MBPP configurations, Sigma repeats 10.4% of its 256 output strings, compared with 53.1% for NLD. Although NLD produces more correct samples per problem on average (139.5 versus 91.5), Sigma produces more distinct correct strings (71.4 versus 46.9), consistent with its later saturation and higher problem coverage.

sections.text: Across MBPP, Minerva Geometry, and GSM8K, CFG and ST expose a broad exploration–exploitation frontier. sections.text: The right panel of Fig. 19 shows the limit of this evidence. Each question therefore requires 32 + 1 32+1 forward passes ( Alg. 2 ). Our implementation evaluates the mean embedding prediction 𝐞 θ = 𝐱 θ ​ 𝐄 {\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}={\mathbf{x}}_{\theta}{\mathbf{E}} on every step (including the final one at t = 0 t=0 which is the argmax readout of the logits that does not require mean embedding prediction), so wall-clock cost is not diluted by that step. The very first denoiser query of each process involves a one-time CUDA initialization which takes a longer time, so is excluded to avoid biasing the measurement. All runs are performed on one H100, using Sigma -3B with precision BF16 . Tab. 20 confirms our claim. At L ′ = 32 L^{\prime}=32 the packed transformer forward costs + 1.8 % +1.8\% over the unguided one, and at L ′ = 64 L^{\prime}=64 it is free to within measurement noise. The per-NFE overhead is dominated by computing the second set of logits, doing softmax, and multiplying by the embedding matrix rather than by attention.

sections.heading: H.1 Supervised Fine-Tuning Setup
sections.text: Our SFT pipeline follows the joint diffusion–AR design of Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion (NLD) ( Fu et al., 2026 ) : the prompt remains clean, supervision is restricted to the response, and the AR and diffusion objectives retain coefficients 1.0 1.0 and 0.3 0.3 , respectively, following the training objective in Sec. 3.2 .

sections.heading: Initialization and objective.
sections.text: We initialize from the 150K-step pretrained Sigma -{3B, 8B} checkpoints, which have block length L ′ = 32 L^{\prime}=32 , separate diffusion and AR readout heads, and self-conditioning. We fine-tune the full transformer and both heads. Let 𝒜 \mathcal{A} denote the supervised answer positions, including the terminal EOS padding described below. The SFT objective is ℒ sft = 0.3 ​ ∑ i ∈ 𝒜 ℒ BD , i | 𝒜 | + ∑ i ∈ 𝒜 ℒ ar , i | 𝒜 | , \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{sft}}=0.3\,\frac{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{A}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{BD},i}}{|\mathcal{A}|}+\frac{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{A}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{ar},i}}{|\mathcal{A}|}, (31) where ℒ BD \mathcal{L}_{\text{BD}} is the continuous block NELBO of 3 and 4 , including its diffusion, reconstruction, and prior terms, and ℒ ar \mathcal{L}_{\text{ar}} is next-token cross-entropy from the clean stream 6 . Each numerator and denominator is summed globally over data-parallel ranks before the two terms are combined. The implementation maintains separate denominators for the two objectives; they are equal in this setup because position zero is an unsupervised system token and both objectives otherwise use the same answer mask. As in pre-training ( Sec. 3.2 ), we estimate the reconstruction and diffusion terms with the Horvitz–Thompson estimator in 5 : independently for each block, we select reconstruction at t = 0 t=0 with probability p rec = 0.1 p_{\mathrm{rec}}=0.1 and otherwise draw t ∼ Unif ⁡ [ 0 , 1 ] t\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,1] . Gaussian noise is applied only in embedding space; the token IDs always remain clean. Prompt and padding positions have zero loss and are pinned to their clean embeddings; answer blocks see the clean context 𝐜 = ( 𝐩 , 𝐫 ( < b ) ) {\mathbf{c}}=({\mathbf{p}},{\mathbf{r}}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}<b})}) of Sec. 4.1 .

sections.heading: Data and preprocessing.
sections.text: Following NLD, our controlled experiment uses the same single-turn SFT dataset of Chandiramani et al. (2026) . Every data sample has system, user, and assistant turns; the system message is empty. The corpus is the non-thinking variant: responses either begin with an empty <think></think> field ( 92.1 % 92.1\% of the samples) or does not have think tags at all. We use the same Mistral-NeMo ( Mistral AI, 2024 ) tokenizer ( V = 131,072 V=131{,}072 ) and the Nemotron Nano chat template ( Blakeman et al., 2025 ) . One key difference between Sigma (continuous diffusion) and NLD (masked diffusion) is that Sigma requires one well-defined diffusion time per block, and thus cannot place prompt and answer tokens in the same noisy block. Therefore, during training, we left-pad each prompt by at most 31 unsupervised tokens so that the answer begins on the absolute 32-token block grid. We do not insert padding between prompt and answer, and inference does not pad the prompt either due to fully causal attention for the prompt. After the answer, supervised EOS tokens complete its final 32-token block; the batch is then right-padded with unsupervised PAD tokens to a multiple of 1024. This coarser batch alignment limits the number of compiled FlexAttention sequence shapes without changing the block factorization.
