sections.heading: Frozen-special-parameter default and ablation.
sections.text: In the main SFT run, we freeze the learned noise-schedule network γ ~ ψ ​ ( t ) \tilde{\gamma}_{\psi}(t) and its endpoints γ 0 , γ 1 \gamma_{0},\gamma_{1} , as well as the diffusion embedding matrix 𝐄 {\mathbf{E}} . This freezes only the continuous-diffusion geometry; the transformer, input and conditioning projections, self-conditioning projection, and both output heads remain trainable at the base learning rate. Our ablation unfreezes the schedule, endpoints, and diffusion embedding matrix while holding all other settings fixed. Following pre-training ( App. E ), these parameters use a 1000 × 1000\times learning-rate multiplier, giving a peak rate of 2.5 × 10 − 3 2.5\times 10^{-3} under the same scheduler; weight decay is zero for the schedule network and diffusion embedding matrix, while the two scalar endpoints retain the base weight decay of 0.1 0.1 .

sections.heading: H.2 Evaluation Setup and Frozen-Parameter Ablation
sections.text: The instruct evaluations in Tabs. 3 and 4 share the diffusion decoder, answer extraction, and seed-error-bar procedure of the base-model harness ( Sec. G.1 ); we describe here only what differs at the instruct operating point.

sections.heading: Benchmarks.
sections.text: We evaluate on ten tasks (numbers in brackets represent the number of problems): GSM8K (1319), MATH-500 (500), AIME 2024 and AIME 2025 (30 each), HumanEval (164), MBPP (378), LiveCodeBench-CPP (454), MMLU (14042), GPQA (198), and IFEval (541). Prompts follow the Nemotron Nano chat template used in SFT training, and the assistant turn is generated in diffusion mode with block length L ′ = 32 L^{\prime}=32 .

sections.heading: Scoring.
sections.text: Math tasks (GSM8K, MATH-500, AIME) are scored by symbolic equivalence on the final \boxed{} answer; GSM8K additionally accepts the last number in the completion. HumanEval and MBPP report executed pass @ ​ 1 @1 on the base test suites (not the + + variants). LiveCodeBench-CPP compiles and runs each extracted C++ program against its tests. GPQA and MMLU are scored by the extracted multiple-choice letter; both are prompted for free-form reasoning ending in Answer: \boxed{A/B/C/D} , and the grader reads the last \boxed{} in the completion, falling back to a regular expression when the model emits none. IFEval reports the instruction-level loose-following rate from the instruction_following_eval checkers, which is the metric the reference models in Tabs. 3 and 4 report.

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: All baseline numbers in Tabs. 3 and 4 are copied from Fu et al. (2026, Tabs. 5, 7) , except that NLD-8B’s diffusion mode results are our reproduction under aligned protocol (without format-injection tricks). Fu et al. (2026) report SDAR-8B Chat at two confidence-threshold operating points (TPF = 1.00 =1.00 and TPF = 1.75 =1.75 ); we use the former as it is stronger on 8 of the 10 tasks (the two exceptions, MMLU and HumanEval, differ by ≤ 0.6 \leq 0.6 points).

sections.heading: Decoding algorithms.
sections.text: We report two operating points, both selected on the base model ( Tab. 1 ) and both with self-conditioning enabled. The DDPM-256 rows use the ancestral sampler on the EDM ρ = 7 \rho=7 schedule with guidance w = 2 w=2 and score temperature τ = 0.1 \tau=0.1 ; the DDIM-32 rows use the deterministic sampler on the uniform- γ \gamma schedule with w = 3 w=3 and τ = 0.3 \tau=0.3 .

sections.heading: Generation budget.
sections.text: Unlike in Fu et al. (2026) who used the same 16834 16834 budget for all tasks, the maximum number of generated tokens for Sigma is set per benchmark rather than uniformly: 1536 1536 for GSM8K, 2560 2560 for HumanEval, MBPP, LiveCodeBench-CPP, and IFEval, 2560 2560 for MMLU, and 4096 4096 for AIME 2024, AIME 2025, MATH-500, and GPQA. These budgets are sized to the per-lane graded-answer-length distribution: on our small-scale smoke runs, no correct answer used a budget beyond 4096 4096 , and the long tail of length is dominated by degenerate repetition that a larger budget does not convert into correct answers.

sections.heading: Seed error bars.
sections.text: As in the base-model harness, each row draws 10 10 independent sampling lanes, averages over questions within each lane to obtain 10 10 per-lane scores, and reports the mean with half-width 2 10 ​ σ ^ \frac{2}{\sqrt{10}}\hat{\sigma} , where σ ^ \hat{\sigma} is the across-lane standard deviation.

We run the comparison at both sampler operating points of Tab. 3 . Under DDPM-256, the two configurations are within the seed interval on seven of ten tasks; under DDIM-32, the ordering of the average reverses, with the unfrozen model ahead. As the two configurations are close in performance in general, we keep the frozen configuration as the simpler default for 8B. sections.heading: I.1 Parallel Predictions and Intra-Segment Rollout
sections.text: PDD reduces the number of expensive denoiser evaluations without discarding the teacher’s fine integration grid. Following Shaul et al. (2026) , we let 1 = t 0 > t 1 > ⋯ > t G = 0 1=t_{0}>t_{1}>\cdots>t_{G}=0 be a decreasing time grid. A conventional DDIM sampler queries the denoiser once per interval and therefore requires G G NFEs. For a target budget M < G M<G , PDD instead partitions the grid into M M segments , 4 4 4 We use segment rather than the term block from Shaul et al. (2026) to avoid confusion with the language-model diffusion blocks. each spanning Δ = G / M \Delta=G/M fine intervals. At the start of segment k k , where i k = k ​ Δ i_{k}=k\Delta , the student evaluates its transformer backbone once and emits Δ \Delta raw clean-embedding predictions required within that segment: 𝐞 ϕ ​ ( 𝐳 i k , t i k , 𝐱 ( < b ) ) = { 𝐞 ^ i k , j S , raw } j = 0 Δ − 1 . \displaystyle{\mathbf{e}}_{\phi}({\mathbf{z}}_{i_{k}},t_{i_{k}};{\mathbf{x}}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}<b})})=\{\hat{\mathbf{e}}^{S,\text{raw}}_{i_{k},j}\}_{j=0}^{\Delta-1}. (32) Here j j is the local offset within the segment, while the corresponding prediction head is indexed by the absolute fine-grid position i k + j i_{k}+j ; we describe this parameterization in Sec. I.2 . All Δ \Delta outputs share the same backbone representation and differ only through lightweight output heads. Because these heads are evaluated in parallel, they cannot consume recurrent self-conditioning from earlier local nodes; we therefore disable self-conditioning for both teacher and student during distillation. Starting from the segment input, these predictions are then composed through the ordinary DDIM recursion DDIM : 𝐳 ~ i k , 0 \displaystyle\tilde{\mathbf{z}}_{{i_{k}},0} = 𝐳 i k , \displaystyle={\mathbf{z}}_{i_{k}}, 𝐳 ~ i k , j + 1 \displaystyle\tilde{\mathbf{z}}_{{i_{k}},j+1} = α i k , j + 1 𝐞 ^ S i k , j + σ i k , j + 1 ⋅ 𝐳 ~ i k , j − α i k , j ​ 𝐞 ^ i k , j S σ i k , j , j = 0 , 1 , … , Δ − 1 , \displaystyle=\alpha_{{i_{k}},j+1}\hat{\mathbf{e}}^{S}_{i_{k},j}+\sigma_{{i_{k}},j+1}\cdot\frac{\tilde{\mathbf{z}}_{{i_{k}},j}-\alpha_{{i_{k}},j}\hat{\mathbf{e}}^{S}_{i_{k},j}}{\sigma_{{i_{k}},j}},\penalty\ j=0,1,...,\Delta-1, (33) where α i k , j = α t i k + j \alpha_{{i_{k}},j}=\alpha_{t_{i_{k}+j}} , σ i k , j = σ t i k + j \sigma_{{i_{k}},j}=\sigma_{t_{i_{k}+j}} , and 𝐞 ^ i k , j S \hat{\mathbf{e}}^{S}_{i_{k},j} denotes the guided student prediction, constructed as follows. The raw prediction in 32 includes the CFG behavior distilled from the teacher but precedes score temperature (ST). Before each solver update, we apply ST analytically using the state 𝐳 ~ i k , j \tilde{\mathbf{z}}_{{i_{k}},j} reached at that local node according to the local DDIM rollout 33 , 𝐞 ^ i k , j S \displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{e}}^{S}_{i_{k},j} = 1 τ ​ 𝐞 ^ i k , j S , raw + ( 1 − 1 τ ) ​ 𝐳 ~ i k , j α i k , j . \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\tau}\hat{\mathbf{e}}^{S,\text{raw}}_{i_{k},j}+\big(1-\frac{1}{\tau}\big)\frac{\tilde{\mathbf{z}}_{{i_{k}},j}}{\alpha_{{i_{k}},j}}. (34) Thus, PDD parallelizes the expensive denoiser predictions, not the inexpensive state updates within a segment. Only the DDIM endpoint 𝐳 ~ i k , Δ \tilde{\mathbf{z}}_{{i_{k}},\Delta} is passed to the next transformer evaluation as 𝐳 i k + 1 {\mathbf{z}}_{i_{k+1}} .

sections.heading: I.2 Residual Parallel Heads
sections.text: Learning to predict an independent clean embedding at every fine-grid node would discard the strong prediction already produced by the pretrained denoiser at each segment start. We instead retain the original diffusion readout as an anchor and parameterize every parallel prediction as a residual transformation of it. Following Shaul et al. (2026) , each residual head is associated with an absolute fine-grid index. Segment k k therefore selects R i k , R i k + 1 , … , R i k + Δ − 1 . \displaystyle R_{i_{k}},R_{i_{k}+1},\ldots,R_{i_{k}+\Delta-1}. (35) Let H ϕ ​ ( 𝐳 i k , t i k , 𝐱 ( < b ) ) H_{\phi}({\mathbf{z}}_{i_{k}},t_{i_{k}};{\mathbf{x}}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}<b})}) be the shared transformer representation from 32 . Its original diffusion readout, which serves as the anchor, is 𝐞 ^ i k S , anchor = softmax ⁡ ( W out ​ H ϕ ​ ( 𝐳 i k , t i k , 𝐱 ( < b ) ) + ℓ prior ​ ( 𝐳 i k , t i k ) ) ​ 𝐄 , \displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{i_{k}}^{S,\text{anchor}}=\operatorname{softmax}(W_{\text{out}}H_{\phi}({\mathbf{z}}_{i_{k}},t_{i_{k}};{\mathbf{x}}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}<b})})+{\bm{\ell}}^{\text{prior}}({\mathbf{z}}_{i_{k}},t_{i_{k}})){\mathbf{E}}, (36) where W out W_{\text{out}} is the vocabulary projection and ℓ prior ​ ( 𝐳 i k , t i k ) {\bm{\ell}}^{\text{prior}}({\mathbf{z}}_{i_{k}},t_{i_{k}}) denotes the output-prior logits. For local offset j j , the corresponding absolute head produces ( 𝐬 i k , j , 𝐫 i k , j ) \displaystyle(\mathbf{s}_{i_{k},j},\mathbf{r}_{i_{k},j}) = R i k + j ​ ( H ϕ ​ ( 𝐳 i k , t i k , 𝐱 ( < b ) ) ) , \displaystyle=R_{i_{k}+j}(H_{\phi}({\mathbf{z}}_{i_{k}},t_{i_{k}};{\mathbf{x}}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}<b})})), 𝐪 i k , j \displaystyle\mathbf{q}_{i_{k},j} = exp ⁡ ( 2 ​ tanh ⁡ ( 𝐬 i k , j ) ) , \displaystyle=\exp(2\tanh(\mathbf{s}_{i_{k},j})), 𝐞 ^ i k , j S , raw \displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{i_{k},j}^{S,\text{raw}} = 𝐪 i k , j ⊙ 𝐞 ^ i k S , anchor + 𝐫 i k , j . \displaystyle=\mathbf{q}_{i_{k},j}\odot\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{i_{k}}^{S,\text{anchor}}+\mathbf{r}_{i_{k},j}. (37) Each R i R_{i} is an embedding-space MLP whose final layer is initialized at zero, so every parallel head initially reproduces the pretrained anchor prediction. The student therefore begins from the pretrained denoiser rather than from randomly initialized parallel predictions, and each residual head only needs to model how the clean prediction evolves along the local trajectory. The additive residual and scaling also allow predictions to leave the convex hull of all token embeddings, which is necessary for matching extrapolated CFG-guided teacher predictions.

sections.heading: I.3 Distillation Objective and Optimization
sections.text: Throughout this subsection, every teacher evaluation is treated as a fixed target: the teacher parameters are frozen, and any student-generated input state is detached at the teacher-query boundary. We omit stop-gradient operators from the notation for simplicity. In contrast, the student evaluation and its intra-segment rollout are constructed with gradients enabled. We distill CFG into the conditional student, while leaving ST as the analytic transformation in 34 . At a student-visited state 𝐳 ~ i k , j \tilde{\mathbf{z}}_{{i_{k}},j} , the frozen teacher’s CFG-guided prediction before ST is 𝐞 ^ i k , j T , raw \displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{e}}^{T,\text{raw}}_{i_{k},j} = 𝐞 T ​ ( 𝐳 ~ i k , j , t i k , j , ∅ ) + w ⁡ [ 𝐞 T ​ ( 𝐳 ~ i k , j , t i k , j , 𝐱 ( < b ) ) − 𝐞 T ​ ( 𝐳 ~ i k , j , t i k , j , ∅ ) ] . \displaystyle={\mathbf{e}}_{T}(\tilde{\mathbf{z}}_{{i_{k}},j},t_{{i_{k}},j};\varnothing)+w[{\mathbf{e}}_{T}(\tilde{\mathbf{z}}_{{i_{k}},j},t_{{i_{k}},j};{\mathbf{x}}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}<b})})-{\mathbf{e}}_{T}(\tilde{\mathbf{z}}_{{i_{k}},j},t_{{i_{k}},j};\varnothing)]. (38) The student receives only the conditional prefix 𝐱 ( < b ) {\mathbf{x}}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}<b})} , so matching this target amortizes the teacher’s conditional and unconditional evaluations into a single student call. Crucially, both 𝐞 ^ i k , j S , raw \hat{\mathbf{e}}^{S,\text{raw}}_{i_{k},j} and 𝐞 ^ i k , j T , raw \hat{\mathbf{e}}^{T,\text{raw}}_{i_{k},j} denote predictions before ST; ST affects the states visited by the local rollout but is not part of the regression target. For each language-model diffusion block b {\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b} , we sample a segment start t i k t_{i_{k}} uniformly from the candidate starts and draw 𝐳 i k {\mathbf{z}}_{i_{k}} from the VP forward marginal conditioned on the clean data embedding. One student evaluation produces the parallel predictions in 32 , from which we construct the differentiable local rollout in 33 . We always supervise the first local node, j 1 = 0 j_{1}=0 , to anchor the segment-start prediction, and sample the remaining P − 1 P-1 indices { j 2 , … , j P } \{j_{2},\ldots,j_{P}\} uniformly without replacement from { 1 , … , Δ − 1 } \{1,\ldots,\Delta-1\} . The PDD objective compares the raw student and CFG-guided teacher predictions at these student-visited states: ℒ PDD \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{PDD}} = 1 P ​ ∑ p = 1 P 𝔼 ⁡ [ ‖ 𝐞 ^ i k , j p S , raw − 𝐞 ^ i k , j p T , raw ‖ 2 ] . \displaystyle=\frac{1}{P}\sum_{p=1}^{P}\E[\|\hat{\mathbf{e}}^{S,\text{raw}}_{i_{k},j_{p}}-\hat{\mathbf{e}}^{T,\text{raw}}_{i_{k},j_{p}}\|^{2}]. (39) This construction is intra-segment on-policy: although the segment start is sampled from the forward marginal, all later supervised states within the segment are generated by the current student. The teacher therefore corrects the student where it locally visits, rather than only on teacher or forward-process states. Because trajectory distillation supervises only the trajectory and only on a sparse set of guided states, we additionally match the teacher’s categorical reconstruction and autoregressive distributions to preserve the pretrained model’s behavior. We use forward KL divergences on the corresponding logits: ℒ teacher-rec = 𝔼 𝐳 0 ( b ) ∼ q ⁡ ( 𝐳 0 ( b ) ∣ 𝐱 ( b ) ) ∑ l = 1 L ′ KL ( 𝐱 T l ( 𝐳 0 ( b ) , 0 ; 𝐱 ( < b ) ) ∥ 𝐱 ϕ l ( 𝐳 0 ( b ) , 0 ; 𝐱 ( < b ) ) ) . \mathcal{L}_{\text{teacher-rec}}=\E_{{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})}\sim q({\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})}\mid{\mathbf{x}}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})})}\sum_{l=1}^{L^{\prime}}\operatorname{KL}({\mathbf{x}}_{T}^{l}({\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})},0;{\mathbf{x}}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}<b})})\,\|\,{\mathbf{x}}_{\phi}^{l}({\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})},0;{\mathbf{x}}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}<b})})). (40) ℒ teacher-ar = ∑ l = 1 L ′ KL ( 𝐱 T AR T l ( 𝐱 ( b , < l ) ; 𝐱 ( < b ) ) ∥ 𝐱 ϕ AR l ( 𝐱 ( b , < l ) ; 𝐱 ( < b ) ) ) . \mathcal{L}_{\text{teacher-ar}}=\sum_{l=1}^{L^{\prime}}\operatorname{KL}({\mathbf{x}}_{T_{\text{AR}}^{T}}^{l}({\mathbf{x}}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b},<l)};{\mathbf{x}}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}<b})})\,\|\,{\mathbf{x}}_{\phi_{\text{AR}}}^{l}({\mathbf{x}}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b},<l)};{\mathbf{x}}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}<b})})). (41) By construction, these losses are zero as distillation begins. Together, this yields the combined objective: ℒ distill = λ PDD ​ ℒ PDD + λ teacher-rec ​ ℒ teacher-rec + λ teacher-ar ​ ℒ teacher-ar , \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{distill}}=\lambda_{\text{PDD}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{PDD}}+\lambda_{\text{teacher-rec}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{teacher-rec}}+\lambda_{\text{teacher-ar}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{teacher-ar}}, (42) Teacher and student are initialized from the same checkpoint, after which the teacher remains frozen. We also freeze the embedding matrix and noise schedule so that the teacher trajectory retains a fixed meaning throughout distillation. The student transformer is adapted through LoRA, while the residual heads are optimized directly with a separate learning rate. This separation allows the new heads to learn local corrections without destabilizing the pretrained backbone or diffusion calibration. Full training details and hyperparameters are given in Sec. I.5 .

sections.heading: I.4 Few-Step Inference
sections.text: For a requested NFE budget M M , we evaluate the student at M M segment starts in sequence. At segment k k , the model uses the absolute heads R i k , … , R i k + Δ M − 1 R_{i_{k}},\ldots,R_{i_{k}+\Delta_{M}-1} , where Δ M = G / M \Delta_{M}=G/M , and advances the state through 34 and 33 . Only the segment endpoint is passed to the next transformer evaluation. The student therefore reduces the sequential neural-network depth from G G evaluations to M M , while retaining fine-grid DDIM integration between evaluations.

sections.heading: Training details.
sections.text: We initialize the student from base Sigma -3B (with or without SUSReg regularization, ablation results are shown in Fig. 7 ), which also serves as the frozen distillation teacher. The embedding lookup, vocabulary projection and noise schedule (including terminal points) are frozen. The transformer backbone is adapted with LoRA of rank 128 128 and scaling factor 256 256 using learning rate 10 − 6 10^{-6} . We use a global bank of 32 32 parallel residual heads parameterized by three-layer MLPs of width 384 384 with standard LayerNorm, which use a separate parameter group with learning rate 2.5 × 10 − 6 2.5\times 10^{-6} . We use AdamW with weight decay 1.0, β 1 = 0.9 \beta_{1}=0.9 , β 2 = 0.999 \beta_{2}=0.999 and a batch size of 256 256 . For all parameters, we use gradient clipping value 1.0. The learning rate schedule is Warmup-Stable-Decay over 10K steps: 5% linear warmup to the nominal learning rate value, constant through step 8000, then exponential decay to 10% of nominal learning rate value. We use a fixed clean context of 512 512 tokens, and train on a signal block of 32 32 tokens. We noticed that this hardly impacts distillation results compared to training on all possible context lengths { 0 , 32 , … , 4064 } \{0,32,\dots,4064\} used for pre-training, while simplifying and significantly accelerating distillation. Our student is trained flexibly at M min = 4 M_{\mathrm{min}}=4 and M max = 8 M_{\mathrm{max}}=8 NFE. For NFE-4 results in Fig. 7 in the main paper, the teacher trajectory uses classifier-free guidance w = 4 w=4 and score temperature τ = 0.4 \tau=0.4 swhile for NFE-8 results, the best guidance setting with w = 3 w=3 and τ = 0.3 \tau=0.3 . These were the only guidance settings investigated and were informed by the self-conditioning-disabled teacher DDIM performance at 32 NFEs. We supervise P = 8 P=8 sampled downstream nodes per segment. In ℒ distill \mathcal{L}_{\text{distill}} 42 , the PDD objective component has weight λ PDD = 5.0 \lambda_{\text{PDD}}=5.0 , the teacher-KL regularization on diffusion stream has weight λ teacher-rec = 0.1 \lambda_{\text{teacher-rec}}=0.1 and teacher-KL regularization on the clean AR stream has weight λ teacher-ar = 0.3 \lambda_{\text{teacher-ar}}=0.3 . These weights were chosen to balance the respective gradient norms.

sections.heading: Flexible-NFE head sharing.
sections.text: Following Shaul et al. (2026) , we train one student for a set of inference budgets ℳ = { M min , 2 ​ M min , … , M max } , M max = 2 a ​ M min . \displaystyle\mathcal{M}=\{M_{\min},2M_{\min},\ldots,M_{\max}\},\qquad M_{\max}=2^{a}M_{\min}. (43) For budget M ∈ ℳ M\in\mathcal{M} , one student evaluation advances Δ M = G / M \Delta_{M}=G/M fine-grid intervals before the transformer is evaluated again. Because the residual heads are indexed by absolute fine-grid position, segment k k selects the contiguous slice R i k , … , R i k + Δ M − 1 R_{i_{k}},\ldots,R_{i_{k}+\Delta_{M}-1} . Changing M M changes the segment boundaries and slice lengths while reusing the same backbone and bank of absolute heads. A single student can therefore be evaluated at several NFE budgets without an additional NFE embedding or a separately distilled model for each budget. During training, NFE budgets are stratified across global microbatches so that all values in ℳ \mathcal{M} receive comparable supervision. This exposes the model both to longer, more difficult intra-segment rollouts at low NFE and to shorter rollouts at higher NFE.

sections.heading: Additional results
sections.text: We synthesize the results in Fig. 7 in the main paper for GSM8K, HumanEval and MBPP. All-task results are displayed in Tab. 8 . PDD achieves a clear 2x acceleration from NFE-16 to NFE-8 relative to its self-conditioning-disabled teacher. Compared to the self-conditioning-enabled Sigma -3B-SUSReg model, which obtains the best results for NFE > > 16, PDD achieves a 2 × \times acceleration from NFE-8 to NFE-4, where it boasts a 68% GSM8K flexible-extract accuracy at NFE=4 while the non-distilled models achieve at most 32%. Coding is empirically more NFE-sensitive: PDD allows a more graceful decay as NFE decreases, but NFE-4 pass@1 still falls short of the performance at NFE > > 16. Importantly, initializing the student and frozen teacher from a checkpoint regularized with SUSReg yields much better distillation performance: +4.67pp at NFE-8 and +3.71pp at NFE-4. This confirms the importance of regularizing the embedding geometry in such a few-NFE setup.

S=\{1,2,3,\cdots,9,10\}. 4 4 numbers are randomly chosen from S . S. She wins a prize if at least two of her numbers were 2 2 of the randomly chosen numbers, and wins the grand prize if all four of her numbers were the randomly chosen numbers. The probability of her winning the grand prize given that she won a prize is m n \tfrac{m}{n} where m m and n n are relatively prime positive integers. Find m + n m+n . A: The probability of winning the grand prize given that Jen won a prize is calculated as follows. Jen wins a prize if at least two of her chosen numbers are among the four randomly selected numbers. The grand prize is won if all four of her chosen numbers are among the four chosen numbers. The total number of ways to choose four numbers from the set S = { 1 , 2 , 3 , … , 10 } S=\{1,2,3,\dots,10\} is ( 10 4 ) = 210 \binom{10}{4}=210 . The event that Jen wins a prize occurs when at least two of her four chosen numbers are in the four chosen numbers. The number of favorable outcomes for winning a prize is found by considering the cases where at least two of her four chosen numbers are included in the four chosen numbers. This is equivalent to the number of ways to choose the four chosen numbers such that at least two of Jen’s four chosen numbers are in the four chosen numbers. The number of ways to choose the four chosen numbers with at least two of Jen’s four chosen numbers is calculated by summing the cases for exactly a numbers of Jen’s numbers being included, where a = 2 , 3 , 4 , 4 a=2,3,4,4 : • For a = 2 a=2 : ( 4 2 ) × ( 6 2 ) = 6 × 15 = 90 \binom{4}{2}\times\binom{6}{2}=6\times 15=90 • For a = 3 a=3 : ( 4 3 ) × ( 6 1 ) = 4 × 6 = 24 \binom{4}{3}\times\binom{6}{1}=4\times 6=24 • For a = 4 a=4 : ( 4 4 ) × ( 6 0 ) = 1 × 1 = 1 \binom{4}{4}\times\binom{6}{0}=1\times 1=1 Summing these gives the total number of outcomes where Jen wins a prize: 90 + 24 + 1 = 115 90+24+1=115 . Which of the following four assumptions jointly imply this “impulse” approximation? 1. The interaction current only interacts with individual nucleons. 2. The nucleus is transparent apart from the selected nucleon. 3. The quarks internal to the selected nucleon are non-relativistic. 4. The interaction proceeds as if the selected nucleon experiences no binding forces. A) 1, 2, 3 B) 1, 3, 4 C) 2, 3, 4 D) 1, 2, 4 A: The “impulse” approximation in many-body nuclear calculations assumes that the behavior of a selected nucleon in a nucleus is similar to that of a free nucleon. This approximation is based on the idea that the interaction on the selected nucleon is not significantly affected by the binding forces from the other particles in the nucleus. To justify this approximation, the following assumptions must ensure that the interaction on the selected nucleon is not influenced by the binding forces from the other nucleons: • Assumption 1 : The interaction current only interacts with individual nucleons. This ensures that the interaction does not depend on the collective state of the nucleus but rather only on the individual nucleons. • Assumption 2 : The nucleus is transparent apart from the selected nucleon. This means that the interaction on the selected nucleon is not altered by the presence of the other nucleons, allowing it to be treated as a free nucleon. • Assumption 4 : The interaction proceeds as if the selected nucleon experiences no binding forces. This directly states that the binding forces from other nucleons are ignored, allowing the selected nucleon to behave like a free nucleon. • Assumption 3 (“quarks internal to the selected nucleon are non-relativistic”) is not relevant to this approximation, as it pertains to the internal structure of the nucleon, not the external environment in the nucleus. Thus, the assumptions that jointly imply the impulse approximation are 1, 2, and 4 . Answer: D

To overcome this, we present Sigma , the first large-scale (3B/8B) continuous dLM built on steerable, low-dimensional ODE/SDE latent trajectories. Trained blockwise via likelihood optimization, Sigma jointly denoises Gaussian-corrupted token embeddings while learning an optimal embedding geometry. To accelerate training, Sigma leverages pre-trained weights from autoregressive (AR) models for warm-starting. During inference, we identify classifier-free guidance and score temperature as essential for high-fidelity reasoning and coding. Across comprehensive math reasoning and coding evaluations against state-of-the-art discrete counterparts (masked dLMs and AR baselines), Sigma achieves competitive performance with discrete models on standard benchmarks (e.g., GSM8K, Minerva, HumanEval, MBPP) after pre-training and on challenging reasoning tasks (e.g., MATH-500, AIME) after supervised fine-tuning. Beyond performance parity, we uncover key structural properties unique to continuous dLMs: ( i ) embedding-space steering effectively governs the quality-diversity trade-off, yielding strong pass@ k k performance and ( ii ) continuous trajectories enable graceful degradation for low NFEs and efficient distillation. These establish continuous dLMs as a promising paradigm for efficient language generation. 1 Introduction While diffusion language models (dLMs) enable fast parallel decoding compared to autoregressive (AR) baselines ( Inception Labs et al., 2025 ; Song et al., 2025 ; Fu et al., 2026 ) , dominant discrete dLMs operate in high-dimensional, categorical state spaces (e.g., V ≥ 100 ​ K V{\geq}100\text{K} ) that suffer under limited step budgets and impede trajectory control for complex reasoning and coding tasks. Continuous diffusion offers a principled way to overcome these structural limitations through smooth latent geometries that natively support structured editing ( Meng et al., 2022 ) , flexible ODE trajectory steering ( Lu et al., 2022 ) , and efficient few-step distillation ( Salimans and Ho, 2022 ; Song et al., 2023 ) . Recently, there has been growing interest in continuous diffusion and flow matching for text generation ( Gulrajani and Hashimoto, 2023 ; Dieleman et al., 2022 ; Hu et al., 2026 ; Lee et al., 2026 ; Guo et al., 2026 ; Liang et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026 ) ; see App. A . However, existing methods remain limited in scale ( < 2 ​ B <2\text{B} ) or focus on unconditional generation, lacking evaluations on complex reasoning tasks. Whether continuous dLMs scale to complex conditional reasoning remains open. This is a non-trivial hurdle because continuous models update block embeddings globally, in contrast to the factorized categorical denoising of discrete dLMs that leads to semi-autoregressive token commitment per block. To overcome these limitations, we present Sigma (3B/8B): s cal i ng up G aussian diffusion m odels for l a nguage. We propose a family of continuous dLMs operating over a 16-dimensional embedding space trained blockwise via likelihood optimization. Within each block, the model learns to jointly denoise Gaussian-corrupted token embeddings and to structure an optimal embedding geometry. To scale training, we warm-start the model from existing pre-trained AR weights. For inference, we explore diffusion trajectory sampling, identifying embedding-space Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) and Score Temperature (ST) as crucial ingredients for high-fidelity reasoning and coding. Figure 1 : Left: Inference pipeline. Sigma generates text blockwise via iterative diffusion denoising over 16D continuous latents ( 𝐳 t \mathbf{z}_{t} ) conditioned on a KV-cached prefix ( 𝐜 \mathbf{c} ), followed by categorical readout. Predicted vocabulary probabilities 𝐱 θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , 𝐜 ) \mathbf{x}_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t;\mathbf{c}) map to mean predictions 𝐞 θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , 𝐜 ) \mathbf{e}_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t;\mathbf{c}) in 16D space via categorical reparameterization. Clean embeddings (dots) lie on the 16D unit sphere, while 𝐞 θ \mathbf{e}_{\theta} lies on or within it. Middle: Smooth trajectory enables low-NFE reasoning. GSM8K accuracy vs. NFEs using the optimal sampler per step budget (PDD: Parallel Decoding Distillation). Right: Scaling inference-time compute. Pass@ k k vs. k k on AIME 2025 (solid curves: fixed config across k k ; thin curves: alternative tested configs). Through unified evaluations against state-of-the-art discrete dLMs (e.g., Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion ( Fu et al., 2026 ) , LLaDA ( Nie et al., 2025b ) , Dream ( Ye et al., 2025 ) , SDAR ( Cheng et al., 2026 ) ), we show that Sigma achieves competitive performance across standard math and coding benchmarks (e.g., GSM8K, Minerva, HumanEval, MBPP) and extends well to harder reasoning tasks after supervised fine-tuning (e.g., MATH-500, AIME). Beyond raw accuracy, we highlight two structural properties unique to continuous language diffusion: ( i ) flexible pass@ k k exploration–exploitation control via CFG and ST hyperparameters; and ( ii ) graceful performance degradation under low NFE regimes (16/32) and efficient trajectory distillation for very low NFE regimes (4/8). Together, these properties position continuous diffusion as a promising foundation for fast inference in modern agentic AI. Our key contributions are summarized as follows: • First Large-Scale Continuous dLM: We present Sigma (3B/8B), efficiently trained by warm-starting from pre-trained AR weights, and optimizing a regularized continuous diffusion ELBO. • Competitive Math & Coding: Across six base and ten instruct benchmarks, Sigma achieves competitive performance with state-of-the-art discrete dLMs/ARs on reasoning and coding. • Inference Steering (CFG & ST): By elucidating the inference design space, we show that embedding-space CFG and ST effectively govern the quality-diversity trade-off with minimal latency overhead via single-pass block-causal attention packing. • Low-NFE Robustness: With embedding regularization, Sigma sustains strong quality down to 16 NFEs per block, while trajectory distillation noticeably improves performance at 4–8 NFEs. 2 Background Notation. As with NLD, we adopt the open-sourced pre-training data from Basant et al. (2025) . We use the Mistral-NeMo tokenizer ( V = 131,072 V=131{,}072 ) ( Mistral AI, 2024 ) , batch size 512 512 , and L = 4096 L=4096 . Architecture. Sigma adopts the transformer backbone of NLD and its AR baseline, ensuring the three families are parameter- and FLOP-matched. As with NLD, Sigma uses a block causal attention mask ( Fig. 2(b) ). Sigma uniquely adds a unit-norm 16-dimensional diffusion embedding table with a linear up-projection, a categorical reparameterization mapping V V -dimensional probabilities to low-dimensional soft embeddings, a self-conditioning linear projection, Fourier time conditioning, and a learnable noise schedule (see Sec. 2 ). Together, these account for less than 1 % 1\% of the total parameters. We provide thorough details in App. E . Training. We train our models for 150K steps, following the optimization procedure detailed in App. E . Given a batch size of 512, 150K steps correspond to over 300B tokens. Training consumed ~9,600 and ~19,200 NVIDIA GB200 GPU hours for the 3B and 8B models, respectively. 3.2.2 AR Initialization and Regularization AR Initialization. To evaluate the impact of initialization, we compare pre-training Sigma ( i ) from scratch and ( ii ) from an AR baseline pretrained on 1T tokens. Due to the dimension mismatch between high-dimensional AR embeddings and Sigma ’s 16-dimensional space, we randomly initialize the diffusion embedding layer. As shown in Figs. 3(a) and 3(b) , Sigma -3B ( L ′ = 64 L^{\prime}{=}64 ) with self-conditioning achieves competitive perplexity relative to NLD-3B ( L ′ = 64 L^{\prime}{=}64 ) under both regimes (i) and (ii). However, AR initialization significantly accelerates convergence and yields lower final training loss. AR Regularization. Continuous diffusion training inherently suffers from high gradient variance and slow convergence. To mitigate variance and accelerate optimization, we follow NLD by adding AR regularization, optimizing the joint objective ℒ ar + w diff ​ ℒ BD \mathcal{L}_{\text{ar}}+w_{\text{diff}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{BD}} ( Fig. 3(c) ; see App. E for the w diff w_{\text{diff}} weighting schedule), where ℒ ar = ∑ l = 2 L − log ⟨ 𝐱 θ l ( 𝐱 < l ) , 𝐱 l ⟩ \mathcal{L}_{\text{ar}}={\textstyle\sum}_{l=2}^{L}-\log\langle{\mathbf{x}}_{\theta}^{l}({\mathbf{x}}^{<l}),{\mathbf{x}}^{l}\rangle (6) is computed over the AR stream using causal attention ( Fig. 2 ). This architecture employs two distinct readout heads, with the AR regularization computed exclusively from the AR head. While this dual-head formulation improves auxiliary AR decoding capability, our primary objective remains maximizing diffusion decoding performance. Finally, input sequences utilize AR embeddings for the AR stream and 16D diffusion embeddings for the diffusion stream ( Fig. 2 ), facilitating AR initialization and efficient KV-caching. As shown in Fig. 3(c) , AR regularization significantly improves training stability; with a properly tuned w diff w_{\text{diff}} , it even outperforms pure perplexity optimization for the diffusion stream. This confirms that AR regularization stabilizes training while yielding a higher-quality model. Classifier-free guidance (CFG). CFG ( Ho and Salimans, 2022 ) is the standard tool for class-conditional or text-to-image diffusion models. In CFG, one queries the model twice to obtain a conditional and an unconditional prediction and then linearly extrapolates them.
